#2121. The state of the atmosphere at St James’ Park, Selhurst Park and what can be done?

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Reading Greg McPeake’s article on The Mag (‘Interesting what these Chelsea fans had to say in the pub the other week’ – 1 Nov) about Chelsea fans giving up their season tickets because they’ve become too expensive, made me think about recurring comments on The Mag and elsewhere about Newcastle United fans and the changing demographics inside St James’ Park on match day.

One description that I’ve seen seems to sum up both the change and the general effect this may be having – that we now have a stadium full of spectators rather than fans.

This was part of the case argued by Chris Hall in his article (‘An open letter to Newcastle United fans’ – 8 Nov) which examined in detail what he sees as the changed atmosphere generated nowadays at St James Park and the reasons for that.

Reaction to that article was, unsurprisingly polarised, with people either praising it for hitting the nail on the head or slamming it as uninformed “bobbins”!

Chris was either exposing the reality of the “Fortress SJP” myth, or exposing his own lack of real experience in a frantic effort to blame the Newcastle United fans for the club’s failings. Take your pick.

I’m not setting out to insult or denigrate anyone by bringing up this issue. I’m well aware that, despite the continuing emphasis on growing the commercial side of match day, the stadium is still rammed with tens of thousands of passionate Geordies – but as season ticket holders of long standing they are inevitably growing longer in the tooth. The passion is, maybe, now internalised and reserved for the more extreme moments rather than roaring out in youthful exuberance throughout the match.

Thus speaks the man who hasn’t ventured inside St James’ Park since the day that internalised passion was released to roundly boo off Moussa Sissoko during a dire home defeat to Bournemouth! I would also like to point out, though, that any reservations regarding the home supporters as a body do NOT apply to the away fans who often show up the home supporters in their own grounds.

Anyway, my aim here wasn’t to focus so much on our supporters but to raise the issue in a wider context, using the example of another club who we played recently – Crystal Palace.

Being a self-professed expert on the state of places I don’t actually go to, I have for years regarded Selhurst Park as one of the last bastions (at Premier League level) of the “real” game. An old fashioned stadium in the heart of the local community with what seems to be an energetic and noisy working class fan base. It certainly comes over that way on the TV and I always enjoy the passion and volume of the Palace fans.

Despite their recent trophy successes – or maybe I should be saying BECAUSE of those successes – Palace are currently struggling in the Premier League. Midweek European games on top of season after season selling their best players has finally caught up with them, it would seem. Things have become so bad that they even contrived to lose at home …… to us!

When reading the Palace fans’ post-match comments on The Mag. I was struck by two references in particular regarding the atmosphere. One referred to our supporters completely out-singing theirs and offering up the ditty, “shall we sing a song for you?” I must say, it was noticeable on the TV that our guys were consistently louder than theirs – something I don’t normally expect at Selhurst Park. In contrast with Darren Henderson’s assertion, in what I thought was an excellent article, (‘Newcastle United on the road to nowhere via Putney Bridge’) published on The Mag on Bonfire Night, that our away support has become “stagnant”, my ears confirmed that it was very much vibrant and in full flow at Selhurst Park on this occasion at least.

Some other comments set me off on understanding why this was possible. These other comments referred to the absence of the “HF”. Visitors to Selhurst Park will know that the popular end of the ground is the Holmsdale Road end and that Palace have a tradition of their most committed supporters gathering there and being orchestrated by a core group of “ultras” known as the Holmsdale Fanatics.

Ultras are very much a European phenomenon – the hard core of the home support, inevitably dressed primarily in black and using a variety of aids, such as drums, megaphones, pyrotechnics and “choirmasters”, to increase noise levels and lead the support within the stadium. They are not generally associated with British teams. Indeed, new Palace manager Pierre Sage stated that a key reason he decided to take charge of the club is because it was one of the only clubs in the Premier League that had ultras. He didn’t mention salary ….

The group was founded in December 2005 by a small number of supporters who had attended matches together since childhood in the 1980s. They traditionally stood in Block B of the Holmsdale Road Stand since 1999 but have had a bit of a running battle with the club, especially following stadium regulations introduced as a result of the Taylor report, which they described as restrictive. They have since been relocated within that end of the ground in, I believe, Block E.

It is this group that has been responsible for the organised displays and coordinated support that has generated much of the energy and noise that I have always associated with the Selhurst Park home crowd. However, that has sadly now (for Palace fans at least) come to an end.

On 28 Aug 2026, they announced that they were disbanding. The Sun quoted their spokesman as stating:

“Increasingly driven out by the sky high ticket prices, needless restrictions that are designed to strip away the dignity of supporters and relentless harassment and legal action, many young people are choosing to opt out of a game which seems determined to push them away.

“There needs to be a drastic shift at Palace towards younger fans and a move away from a culture in which people attend the ground expecting to be entertained, towards a culture of supporters turning up to play an active role in influencing the result.”

Ticket price rises forcing traditional, working class supporters and youngsters away. Longstanding supporters having to give up season tickets as referenced by Greg’s Chelsea supporting pals. Youngsters being priced out of match day and being replaced by “tourists” prepared to pay the commercial rates for a one-off experience. These are familiar refrains – not just emanating from Monkseaton but increasingly from all other corners of Geordieland. Spectators rather than fans!

The quote continues, elaborating on the issue of mounting displays and using flags and banners during the match:

“From fighting for the most basic of rights just to take materials into Selhurst and stand up in Block B in the early days, to never ending problems with the club right up to the present day, we have been uncompromising in fighting for what we believe in and the rights of football supporters everywhere.”

At St James’ Park, Wor Flags suspended their activities due to Mike Ashley and his lack of support for Rafa Benitez in particular. Fortunately, they were not just welcomed back by the new owners but positively encouraged.

The Holmsdale Fanatics have clearly not enjoyed that kind of relationship with the Palace hierarchy. For whatever reason, I would argue that this has been to the detriment of the club because of the consequent deterioration, now, in the match day atmosphere.

Another key issue that crops up in relation to clubs throughout the country is an inevitable outcome of the aforementioned Taylor Report and that is the fact that, due to the requirement for grounds to be all seater, it is impossible for groups of like-minded supporters to simply gather together within the stadia and choose where they sit/stand (even in home areas of safe standing).

“But the current set up is unsustainable. We have repeatedly warned the club that like-minded fans cannot congregate at Palace in the numbers required to sustain a growing active supporter culture.”

My last visit to SJP, to the ill-fated Bournemouth match mentioned above, required an expedition to the heights of Level 7. Probably the “final frontier” of like-minded congregation, Kind Mike put a stop to it all by relocating the season tickets to other parts of the ground. That despite them serenading him with his own special song! It seems to me as an external observer since then that the atmosphere hasn’t been the same.

The BBC on 28 Aug 2026 carried the Holmesdale spokesman’s reference to the away day experience. It sounds quite bleak but I don’t think it mirrors the experience of our own fans judging by comments I read on The Mag and elsewhere.

“The story away from home is even more dire. In domestic away fixtures, supporters are banned from bringing materials into stadiums, coaches are regularly stopped, and fans are arrested. Away ends across the country are increasingly dominated by older fans, with the next generation failing to come through in significant numbers.”

As I mentioned earlier in the article, our away supporters seem to have a fair proportion of younger lads in their midst – something confrmed for me by my special correspondent, Mr Tony Malabar, who travels away to every game.

The Palace quotes end with a note of pride, however:

“Given these conditions, we have immense pride in all the group has achieved over the past 20 years. From being at the heart of the protests that rescued the club in 2010, to securing the away ticket price cap that has saved working class people millions and supporting the club through a record breaking period, the Holmesdale Fanatics has helped write a chapter in the club’s history that many did not believe was possible.”

They say that they will continue to attend matches but just as a group of mates rather than an organised “ultras” group.

So what? That’s Crystal Palace not us! Or is it?

I freely admit to being an armchair fan. I have never had a season ticket. In my younger days I couldn’t afford it and, anyway, preferred to play sport rather than watch it. Later, I had what I considered more pressing family commitments and moved away to work elsewhere in the country. I now live about 800 hundred miles South West of Newcastle.

My impressions are necessarily gained via Sky/TNT Sports, what my few season ticket-holding mates have to say and conversations on the likes of The Mag. They may well be accurate but could just as easily be wide of the mark. It would therefore be interesting to read your comments in response to the article.

Has the game gone? Have individual seats left aged, ex boot boys too exposed to express themselves? Are the Instagram day trippers taking over? Is the bubble set to burst?

Should we all be singing an altered refrain from the Palace club anthem?

“You say that you love (Say you love me) All of the time (All of the time) You say that you need me (Say you need me) You’ll always be mine (Always be mine) I’m Feeling Sad All Over Baby I’m Sad All Over ….”

#2120. Rare moment of of sanity from pundit – offers shrewd advice for for West Ham’s worried army

There’s a certain perspective on this weekend’s defeat now, the dust having settled on the Ewood Park 2-1 loss and the furious away fans now returned back to their day jobs. In the cold light of day this would seem to be a drama, not a crisis – West Ham are ninth in the division, sure, but still just six points off second spot.

Defeats have been bad, but it is not yet disaster time, according to talkSPORT’s Jason Cundy

It shows the hugely competitive nature of this league, true, but suggests that with Kretinsky’s swift action to replace Nuno with former Hammer Scott Parker, West Ham have acted in time to save themselves.

That is certainly the view of Jason Cundy, talk SPORT pundit and former Chelsea and Tottenham regular who is quite happy to stick the boot in to the Hammers. Unnervingly, in this instance he’s helped bring a dash of stability to Hammers’ fans’ woes. Yahoo Sport’s article confirms – Cundy is still a believer:

“Maybe it’s just me being deluded but I still think West Ham will be there or thereabouts come the end of the season. It’s a bad result (against Blackburn Rovers), you cannot deny that and Scotty Parker has come in, he’s got a bit of work to do. West Ham are now 9th. They’re only six points off 2nd place. It’s not a disaster this.”

Yes there’s a drama at east London, as most neutral’s favourites for automatic promotion continue to stumble. But six points can easily be recovered over the hectic schedule in the run up to Christmas. Maybe a reminder to us all to take a breath, check the table again at the end of the year – and let Scott Parker do his thing in the meantime.

Thomas Tuchel announced his latest England squad on Friday.

This was for the November internationals in the Nations League.

The England squad taking on Croatia and Spain.

Lewis Hall was named in Friday’s squad (see below).

Now the Newcastle United left-back has been joined by Dan Burn.

The FA official England squad announcement this Monday morning:

Dan Burn has been added to the England squad following the withdrawal of Marc Guéhi through injury.

#2115. Sam Johnstone's honest Celtic results admission as dressing room mood revealed

Goalkeeper Sam Johnstone admits Celtic have fallen below expectations this season, with recent form impacting the team's spirit.

Thursday's 3-2 victory over Besiktas, Johnstone says, showed their character, with the long-term target now to 'put things right'.

The stopper, signed on loan from Wolverhampton Wanderers during the summer transfer window, has started Celtic's last five matches, displacing Viljami Sinisalo between the sticks.

"The expectation, rightly so, for this place is to win games," Johnstone said. "Unfortunately, we hadn't quite met that expectation, and the lads know that. We try to win every game and put things right."

Celtic goalkeeper Sam Johnstone walks off the pitch at half-time. (Image: Stuart Wallace / Shutterstock)

Celtic had won just three of their previous ten matches before Besiktas.

Beating the Turks, then, was crucial in repairing the mood, both internally and externally.

"I think the results affect it," Johnstone said of the spirit within the camp. "This club's not used to losing, and we’ve probably lost too many games for this club.

"We all realise that, but we have to put things right in each game. The lads go out to win every game, so the camp is good.

"It was tough. We're honest players, we're honest people, and honest with each other. You could see on Thursday night that the lads put a good fight in and got the result."

Johnstone's recent run of starts is his most consistent since joining Celtic at the start of September.

The 33-year-old was thrust in shortly after signing, playing against St Johnstone in the William Hill Premiership and Rangers in the Premier Sports Cup.

He failed to impress in the 3-0 defeat at Ibrox but now looks far more assured.

"To get a run of games for any player, you find your rhythm," Johnstone explained. "It was a new club for me, a new team, so that takes probably a couple of games to get used to as well.

"Listen, to get the games and to keep going and get the win on Thursday night was a good feeling.

"It's brilliant to play for this club. The passion of the fans, good and bad. The standard of players on the pitch, day in, day out at training.

"When I came, I said I didn't have to think twice about coming here."

After their first Europa League win of the season, Celtic's focus shifts back to the domestic scene, where Kilmarnock lie in wait on Sunday afternoon.

Returning to winning ways in the Premiership after last weekend's defeat to Falkirk is key.

#2113. ‘I like him a lot’ – Romelu Lukaku has been mindblown by Liverpool player he could face tonight

Romelu Lukaku has joined the ever-growing fan club of teenage Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha, having been impressed by what he’s seen from the 18-year-old.

The youngster has earned widespread praise for his effervescent performances since breaking into the Reds’ first team last year and has started all three Champions League games so far under Andoni Iraola.

He had to be content with 25 minutes or so off the bench against Arsenal on Sunday and was kept quiet by a sturdy Gunners defence, but his direct running has left an impression on the experienced Belgian striker, who he’ll face tonight in our European clash against Fenerbahce.

Lukaku was speaking to TNT Sports ahead of the fixture at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium, and he highlighted the threat that Liverpool pose in midfield and attack, with the 33-year-old singling out Ngumoha for praise.

The ex-Manchester United and Everton marksman said: “Offensively they are very good as well. I like Rio. I like him a lot, very direct. I saw his game that he played against Arsenal.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Ngumoha gave arguably his best Liverpool performance in their most recent Champions League outing, the 4-3 win over Villarreal a fortnight ago when he tormented the LaLiga side in completing seven out of the eight dribbles that he attempted (Sofascore).

In many ways he’s almost the antithesis of Lukaku, who’s a towering target man more renowned for power than pace, but the Fenerbahce striker is no less admiring of the teenage winger’s qualities.

The 18-year-old has exuded fearlessness ever since his first-team breakthrough at Anfield, and we highly doubt he’d be overawed by the febrile atmosphere of the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium if he starts tonight.

If Ngumoha can deliver another big performance for Liverpool in Istanbul and the Reds maintain their 100% Champions League record under Iraola, the case for tying him down to a bumper new contract would be strengthened even further.

#2111. First meeting against a team 20 unbeaten: All the key stats ahead of Milan vs. Ferencvaros

The first ever competitive meeting between AC Milan and Ferencvaros will take place at San Siro this evening in the Europa League.

Milan have played four times in history against Hungarian opponents. The first time was in the 1967-68 Cup Winners’ Cup, when the Rossoneri draw 2-2 away and 1-1 at home against ETO, which saw them progress on away goals.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The other two occasions came 15 years later in the 1982 Mitropa Cup group stage against Szombathelyi Haladas. The Diavolo won both encounters: 2-0 at San Siro, and 1-0 away from home.

So, tonight’s contest is an unprecedented one, and it pits two teams together that have made very different starts to their Europa League campaigns.

➤ Alphadjo Cisse has caught the eye for Milan in Europa League play. The striker is the side’s top scorer with three goals, which is joint most in the competition, one of those having been the critical first of the match.

➤ Kristoffer Zachariassen has been the most prolific player for Ferencváros, scoring on three occasions in the current Europa League campaign, including one match-opening goal. He is tied as the competition’s top scorer in 2026-27.

➤ The Rossoneri secured an impressive 3-1 victory over city rivals Inter at the weekend, strengthening their position in the Serie A top-four race. Milan have lost just once in their opening ten league matches, recording six victories and three draws, although their continental performances have been considerably less convincing.

➤ The Diavolo suffered a comprehensive 3-0 defeat away to Bournemouth on matchday three, leaving them with two losses from their opening three Europa League fixtures and only one victory in their last six European matches overall.

➤ Milan’s struggles have extended to home soil, where they lost 2-0 against Benfica in their only previous Europa League fixture at the Giuseppe Meazza this season. Another defeat would see them lose consecutive European home matches within a single campaign for the first time since 2010/11.

➤ Nevertheless, their recent attacking form offers some encouragement: five of their last six competitive matches have produced at least three goals, and Amorim’s side has scored before the 25th minute in each of their previous four home fixtures.

➤ Ferencváros, by contrast, have enjoyed an outstanding start to their European campaign, winning all three league-phase matches and scoring freely along the way. Their most recent outing produced a convincing 4-1 victory over Torreense, with Bamidele Yusuf, Mariano Gómez and Krisztián Lisztes among the scorers. Balázs Borbély’s side have now won five of their last six competitive matches, drawing the other, and have scored 18 goals while conceding just four during that sequence.

➤ The Hungarian champions are unbeaten in 20 competitive matches since late July, recording 13 victories and seven draws, while each of their last four wins has come by at least two goals. They also boast an impressive away record, having avoided defeat in their last ten competitive matches on the road and conceded no more than once in any of those fixtures.

➤ Victory in Milan would see Ferencváros win four consecutive matches in major European competition for the first time since the 1967-68 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, when they recorded six successive victories on their way to the final.

➤ This will be the first competitive meeting between Milan and Ferencváros, although both clubs have limited historical experience against opposition from the other’s country. Milan’s only previous European encounters with Hungarian opponents came against Győri ETO in the 1967/68 Cup Winners’ Cup, with both matches ending level.

➤ Ferencváros, meanwhile, have failed to win any of their last four European away fixtures against Italian teams, drawing twice and losing twice, since defeating Roma in the 1965 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup. With Milan seeking to revive their European campaign and the visitors determined to preserve their perfect record, both sides have considerable motivation heading into this encounter.

#2110. SPFL round-up: Partick Thistle go top as Hamilton stunned by Cove Rangers

Partick Thistle climbed to the top of the William Hill Championship with a 1-0 victory over rock-bottom Queen’s Park.

The moment of the game came 10 minutes after the break when Seb Drozd’s effort deflected to Tony Watt at the far post who headed Thistle to victory and climbed above Raith who drew 0-0 with Dunfermline.

Dylan Borso scored four times as they came from behind to win 4-3 and inflict a fourth straight defeat on Stenhousemuir despite playing more than an hour with a man less after Calvin Okike was sent off for the hosts.

Arbroath ended a run of five-straight defeats in style as they earned a convincing 4-1 win over Ayr courtesy of goals from Thomas O’Brien, Michael McKenna, Gavin Reilly and Jacob MacIntyre.

Cristian Montano’s equaliser cancelled out Alfie Stewart’s opener as Livingston drew 1-1 with Inverness.

In League One, Ross County moved five points clear at the top of the league after they ran out 4-1 winners over Peterhead.

Brian Graham and Chris Hamilton gave County a 2-0 lead before Mitch Megginson pulled a goal back for the visitors but the home side finished the job with further goals from Richard Chin and Kieran Phillips’ penalty.

Second-placed Hamilton suffered a shock first defeat of the season after they were thrashed 4-0 by rock-bottom Cove Rangers thanks to Edimond Oppong’s hat-trick and Joseph Teasdale’s late strike.

Goals from Jamie Hamilton and Cameron Elliott’s penalty helped East Kilbride come from behind and earn a first win four games with a 2-1 victory over Queen of the South.

Cammie Ross struck four minutes from time to give East Fife a second-straight win as they beat Montrose 2-1 who had goalscorer Blair Lyons sent off late.

Airdrieonians ended a run of three consecutive defeats with a 3-2 win over lowly Alloa courtesy of Rangers loanee Josh Gentles’ late goal.

Stranraer remained at the top of League Two with a 3-0 victory over Stirling who saw their five-match league unbeaten run come to an end.

Second-placed Clyde picked up a third win from their last four after they twice came from behind to beat The Spartans 3-2.

Leighton McIntosh and Scott Honeyman gave Dumbarton a first win in four with a 2-0 victory over Elgin.

Jack Brydon’s late strike earned Kelty Hearts a 2-1 win over Annan Athletic while Forfar drew 1-1 with Edinburgh.

#2109. ‘Big call’ – Journalists react as Iraola names ‘exciting line-up’ for Liverpool in Istanbul

Andoni Iraola has made five changes to the Liverpool starting XI for tonight’s Champions League clash against Fenerbahce, with the head coach not afraid to drop some big names to the substitutes’ bench.

A relentless fixture list and a quick turnaround from the defeat to Arsenal on Sunday has no doubt been a factor in Iraola making so many changes, but it’s by no means a weak starting XI for Liverpool.

#2108. GdS: A combined salary less than Ramos’ – the story behind the Ferencvaros ‘miracle’

AC Milan’s opponents Ferencvaros are one of a few teams to have a perfect record in the Europa League, and their story is a fascinating one.

Ferencváros arrive at San Siro having won all three of their league phase games thus far. In addition to that, they are 20 unbeaten across all competitions and they will go top of their domestic league if they win their game in hand. La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) share some insight on the Hungarians.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Gonçalo Ramos’s gross salary €12.8m (€7m net including bonuses) is equivalent to the entire wage bill of Ferencváros. The combined salaries of the Hungarian club’s players total €11m.

Their highest earner is Naby Keïta, who accepted a contract worth just over €1.2m gross per season, seeking a career resurgence at the club with the largest payroll in the Hungarian league.

The Serbian midfielder Birmančević – formerly of Sparta Prague and Getafe, who arrived last summer – earns a slightly lower salary. Meanwhile, attacking midfielder Zachariassen earns around €700k and has scored three goals so far, as has Alphadjo Cissé.

In terms of wages, therefore, there is simply no comparison between the Rossoneri and Ferencváros. Yet, the Hungarians have won every match, while Milan have only three points. All the more reason not to take them lightly.

Gabor Kubatov has been on the board of Ferencváros since 2010, becoming president a year later. Under his leadership, the club has won eight Hungarian league titles. His personal history is quite unique: as a young man, he was a regular in ‘Sector 2’ – the section occupied by the ultras.

He later changed paths, and in 2006, he became a member of parliament, representing Fidesz, the party of Viktor Orbán. Despite his own background in the stands, his relationship with the Ferencváros ultras has not always been smooth.

In 2014, in an effort to combat violence and incidents of racism, Kubatov introduced a biometric identification system for stadium entry. A segment of the most ardent supporters responded by boycotting home matches, a protest that lasted for over three years.

An agreement was finally reached and the fans returned to the stands. With their support, Ferencváros went on to win seven consecutive league titles.

On 10 December 2017, a young Adam Nagy faced Milan while playing for Bologna. It didn’t go well: a 2-1 victory for the Rossoneri. Today, Nagy returns as a far more mature leader of his ‘miracle’ Ferencváros side.

Indeed, a significant portion of the Hungarian midfielder’s career has unfolded in Italy. He spent three years with the Rossoblù from 2016 to 2019 – following his initial breakthrough at Ferencváros – before returning to Italy in 2021 to join Pisa, having previously left to try his hand at Bristol City in England.

His most recent stint was with Spezia, which he departed this summer to return to his homeland. Yesterday, in a press conference, Rúben Amorim spoke very highly of him: “He is very skilled in the initial phase of build-up play.”

His ability to circulate the ball deep in his own half is his greatest strength. Conversely, he rarely ventures into the final third. The proof? Throughout all his years in Italy, he scored only one goal: against Verona in Serie A.

From the European champions Liverpool to Ferencvaros. Naby Keita – who will start on the bench tonight, hasn’t had the career he hoped for. Liverpool paid €65m to sign him from RB Leipzig in 2018, he won six more trophies in addition to the Champions League with Klopp’s English side.

In 2023, the Guinean midfielder moved to Werder Bremen, where he was left out of the squad after refusing to travel for the trip to Leverkusen because he wouldn’t have been a starter. Since January 2025, he has been at Ferencváros, who acquired him a year later.

Wearing a Liverpool shirt, Keïta has already beaten Milan at San Siro on 7 December 2021, a defeat that contributed to the Diavolo being eliminated in the group stage.

A less pleasant memory for Keïta involves his encounter with Luka Modrić when he came on in the final minutes of the 2022 Champions League final, which Liverpool lost to Real Madrid.

#2107. ‘Not good’ – Ally McCoist slams Liverpool star after mistake which left teammate ‘livid’

Ally McCoist was critical of one Liverpool player for his unwitting role in Fenerbahce’s equaliser against the Reds in the first half of their Champions League game on Wednesday.

The away side took a well-deserved lead in the 25th minute when Trey Nyoni’s deflected shot sailed into the net, with the teenage midfielder being credited with his first official goal in senior football.

However, the hosts restored parity just four minutes later, and again it was with the aid of a deflection as Mason Greenwood’s free kick hit off Jeremy Jacquet and was diverted into the net, with Alisson Becker not disguising his rage at the defensive wall in front of him.

Speaking on co-commentary for TNT Sports (via BBC Sport), McCoist called out the French defender for turning his back on the ball as the set piece was struck.

The Scotsman said: “I think the goalkeeper will not be too happy with his wall. Alisson is livid. Jeremy Jacquet turns his back. You have to stand up and take it. Not good defending.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The summer arrival from Rennes has been excellent in his time at Liverpool so far, rightly receiving plenty of praise for his performances and winning his first senior call-up for France, but he won’t be happy with his part in Greenwood’s rather fortuitous equaliser.

The normally teak-tough 21-year-old paid a heavy price for turning his back on the ball, even if nobody could legislate for the huge stroke of luck that Fenerbahce received.

He’s also met his physical match in Romelu Lukaku, with the Belgian striker standing up to Jacquet in a way that few (if any) Premier League forwards have managed since the start of this season.

If Liverpool were pegged back by a piece of brilliance which was near-impossible to defend, we’d be able to accept it, but the manner of Greenwood’s goal (and it had to be him, didn’t it?) will rankle as much with Andoni Iraola as it did with the visibly furious Alisson.

At the time of writing, hopefully the centre-back and his team can put that regrettable moment behind them and go on to take all three points home to Merseyside.

#2105. GdS: Milan’s €500m Adidas deal causes reaction from rivals Inter – the situation

Inter are looking enviously at their city rivals AC Milan once again after Saturday’s derby, with the news of the record Adidas deal emerging.

As reported by La Gazzetta dello Sport on Wednesday, under the new agreement Adidas will pay Milan €50m per year for ten seasons starting from 2028-29. This is when the collaboration with PUMA ends, who currently pay €24.5m per year, as per the last accounts.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The paper (via Calciomercato.com) go on to state that it is likely that the €50m yearly figure includes sporting bonuses, such as participation in the Champions League, the value of material supplies (value in kind) and a portion to be invested in promotional activities (marketing fund).

Contracts with kit makers are not limited to recognising the value of just the home, away, third and other shirts, but can extend to the sale of related products. Then, guaranteed minimums and royalties come into play that are triggered above a certain turnover threshold.

For example, in addition to the €24.5m from PUMA, €55.8m in revenues came from store, e-commerce and merchandising/licensing activities, in particular those relating to the contract with the same German company and those from licensing with Fanatics and MatchWornShirt.

As for Inter, the renewal with Nike – effective from 2023 – resulted in a 70% increase over the previous contract, but the €28m per year is not in line with the club’s current commercial value. In addition to the Milan-Adidas deal, Juventus currently get €46m per year from Adidas (€41m from 2027-28).

Inter have maintained their merchandising revenues internally, over €35m in 2025-26 thanks to the new business model introduced with Fanatics, but Nike’s €28m is too little according to the Nerazzurri’s commercial management.

The contract expires in 2031, and La Gazzetta report that they will seek to renegotiate the deal to avoid accumulating delays over the next five years. Considering that Juventus and Milan have committed to the next decade, Inter have leverage as the only one of the ‘big three’ up for grabs.

#2104. ‘Soft’ – Stephen Warnock takes aim at Liverpool star who ‘cost his side’ against Fenerbahce

Stephen Warnock was critical of one Liverpool player over the concession of a ‘soft goal’ in their Champions League clash against Fenerbahce on Wednesday.

The Reds had the lead twice at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium, with Trey Nyoni and Alexander Isak netting for Andoni Iraola’s side, but the midfielder’s goal was swiftly cancelled out by a deflected Mason Greenwood free kick.

The home side equalised again through Archie Brown and had the final say with a Vedat Muriqi header which secured all three points.

The second Fenerbahce goal had Warnock pointing the finger of blame at Alisson Becker for not coming to claim the ball from the cross which led to the left-back’s leveller.

Speaking on MOTD: UEFA Champions League for BBC Sport, the former Liverpool defender said: “That’s another soft goal conceded by Liverpool but this one was more down to Alisson not coming to claim the ball – and either cleaning out Gakpo or letting him know he is coming.

“I just watched the replay and there was definitely no shout… that’s a lack of concentration from the goalkeeper, and it has cost his side.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Alisson had bailed out his teammates a couple of times earlier in the match after some sloppy errors just outside the penalty area, but the goalkeeper won’t be happy with his involvement in Brown’s equaliser.

He was unusually hesitant in coming for the ball as the cross was played in, although he doesn’t bear sole culpability for a cheap goal for Fenerbahce.

Cody Gakpo was unlucky that his attempted headed clearance went backwards, but Dominik Szoboszlai completely switched off to allow the left-back to run in behind him and have a simple finish from close range.

#2103. St Johnstone boss banishes Dundee demons with ‘bitter’ declaration

Simo Valakari was thrilled to give St Johnstone supporters a 2-1 victory over Dundee to celebrate after recent Perth struggles against their Tayside rivals.

Dundee won twice at McDiarmid Park in 2024-25, the season Saints were relegated, but a transformed team has returned to the top flight under Valakari.

They drew level on 17 points with Dundee in the William Hill Premiership thanks to a fourth win of the season. Valakari lapped up the success, with fans joyous at a first home victory over the Dark Blues since October 2021.

“We are a totally new team and it is not good to hold on to all those memories,” said Valakari. “Me as a manager, of course I remember. At Christmas-time we were 3-0 down after 20 minutes of the biggest game of the season.

“And of course I remember when their fans were on the pitch celebrating on the last day. But my players don’t have this baggage. We are creating new experiences together; this is our new adventure.

“If I carried everything that happened in the past with me, I would be a very bitter person! You need to let things go; that’s why we didn’t even bring it up.

“But all the players knew how much this game meant to our fans. We needed to perform, and we did. And to perform the way we did against a very good team made it a deserved win.”

Josh Campbell headed Saints in front after five minutes before substitute Joe Westley replied early in the second half following a mix-up between goalkeeper Ross Sinclair and Cheick Diabate. Kai Fotheringham, on his first Premiership start for Saints, netted a deflected winner in the 72nd minute.

“We were very good in the first half,” said Valakari. “They changed things at half-time. It took us a bit of time to adjust and we conceded a goal in that period.

“My team showed their character and personality again. We got control back and it got better and better from that.”

Dundee manager Steven Pressley conceded that his team failed to match much of their early-season form. He admitted St Johnstone were deserving winners over the course of the match.

“Over the course of the 90 minutes, St Johnstone were probably deserving of the victory,” he said. “We didn’t quite reach the heights and the standards that we’ve set.

“It’s not a criticism, it’s just these players continuously produced really high performances and have set some incredible standards. We were just a little bit below them on some of the things that we pride ourselves on.

“And, on the things we pride ourselves on, I thought St Johnstone were very strong. We’re disappointed to go into an international break on a defeat.”

#2102. ‘They deserve it’ – Kostas Tsimikas admits familiar failing cost Liverpool in Istanbul

Kostas Tsimikas admitted that Liverpool got what they deserved in their 3-2 defeat to Fenerbahce in Istanbul on Wednesday.

The Reds were in front twice at the Sukru Saracoglu Stadium but still contrived to come away with nothing against Dirk Kuyt’s side, who claimed all three points thanks to Vedat Muriqi’s 79th-minute header.

Jeremy Jacquet was criticised for turning his back on Mason Greenwood’s free kick for the first equaliser, and Alisson Becker was culpable of poor positioning for Archie Brown’s goal to make it 2-2.

Speaking to UEFA.com after the match, Tsimikas magnanimously conceded that Fenerbahce were full value for their win and lamented Liverpool’s defending over the goals that they shipped.

The Greek defender said (via BBC Sport): “Congratulations to Fenerbahce, they deserve it. We didn’t play how we had to play. We didn’t defend after the goal we conceded. After three or four minutes, automatically we conceded another goal.

“I think we have to mark better if we want to win games. We didn’t play very good and that’s why we lost.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

It sums up how careless Liverpool were this evening that they were in the lead twice and occupied a winning position for only eight minutes against Fenerbahce, with the goals from Trey Nyoni and Alexander Isak cancelled out all too quickly.

The manner of all three goals that the home side scored will enrage Iraola – it wasn’t as though the Istanbul outfit had to produce moments of magic to inspire their way to victory over the Reds.

Tsimikas himself was far from convincing, enduring a ‘tough night’ in the words of Liverpool Echo reporter Paul Gorst as he struggled to contain the threat of Greenwood, and he ended up being substituted for Milos Kerkez with 15 minutes remaining.

Liverpool have now conceded 10 goals in their four Champions League matches, shipping three for the third European fixture in a row, a record which’ll surely concern the head coach at this phase of the competition.

The debrief from this game will not be a pleasant one, and a much better defensive performance will be required if the Reds are to return to winning ways against Crystal Palace on Sunday.

#2099. Jim Goodwin bites tongue with ‘careful’ admission after VAR intervention

Boss Jim Goodwin hit out at the decision to award the penalty that cost Dundee United dear in a 1-1 draw against Motherwell at Tannadice.

Referee Ryan Lee had initially given a free-kick for offside in the early stages of the game.

However, he was then advised by VAR Andrew Dallas to have another look at an incident where Tawanda Maswanhise had gone down in the United box under a challenge by home skipper Dylan Tait.

After checking the pitchside monitor, the whistler pointed to the spot with Motherwell captain Lukas Fadinger tucking the penalty away.

The Terrors ultimately salvaged a point thanks to a Jesse Randall goal but Goodwin insisted his side should have had all three.

He said: “It’s a poor decision for me. I know it’s going to be subjective and people will have their own opinions on it, but I don’t know what Dylan Tait is meant to do.

“We all know Maswanhise runs at pace, he’s driving at the defender and I think he’s going down before the contact arrives.

“Dylan is pulling out and I just don’t understand what a defender is meant to do in that situation.

“The linesman initially was giving an offside but neither he or the ref thought there was a foul in that particular instance.

“We were happy with that but when VAR check it there’s not the offside and they decide to carry on the check into the penalty incident.

“I need to be careful what I say because I got in trouble a few years ago talking about players going over easily in the penalty area.

“But I think a bit of experience, knowing the type of players you’re dealing with, the referee at that moment made the right call.

“When the referee got called to the monitor, you have an experienced referee there basically telling a young ref he’s made a mistake.

“So it takes a bit of courage for the ref on the park to overrule that decision from the VAR room. It’s gone against us but we reacted positively.”

Not surprisingly, Motherwell manager Alfred Johansson disagreed with Goodwin’s assessment of the penalty decision and instead insisted it should have been awarded.

The 36-year-old said: “I haven’t watched it back with a close-up on the situation in the box yet but the way I saw it JT (Maswanhise) is running at high speed into the box. He’s on the ball and gets down from a tackle, and it’s a penalty.

“So it depends on who you ask. None of us can complain with the draw, it was a very tight game. It was very open but definitely fair with the draw.”

#2097. Rangers face battle to keep Ryan Naderi after source's scout reveal - verdict

Senior Correspondent AUTHORITY Sports journalist with experience at Football League World and Burton Albion FC; Derby University graduate. FOCUS Transfer coverage and behind-the-scenes insight across the Premier League, EFL, and SPFL. THE INSIGHT Evan utilises a network of club and industry contacts to deliver verified, high-speed transfer reporting. He provides the depth behind the deals to ensure fans get the full story as it happens.

Rangers are sure to find it increasingly difficult to keep hold of striker Ryan Naderi as his impressive form continues in the Scottish Premiership.

The Czech international has been like a man transformed at Ibrox so far this season, and is quickly becoming one of the first names on the teamsheet.

In the absence of Youssef Chermiti, the 23-year-old has stepped up and taken on the attacking burden for Derek McInnes' side, and to great effect of late.

Naderi is the Gers' top scorer in league action so far with six strikes, while his tally of nine goals in all competitions has already set a new best for a single season in his career.

The former Hansa Rostock man is finally beginning to prove himself at Ibrox, but that will naturally be attracting attention from elsewhere.

With Naderi's stock beginning to rise consistently in recent weeks, it surely won't be long before Rangers have to worry about losing him.

Naderi is in a simply remarkable vein of form at Rangers right now, and is spearheading their push for the league title.

Across his last 10 club games, the young forward has seven goals and three assists to his name, and has played almost every minute for his team.

McInnes is placing great importance on him right now, and his faith in Naderi is being repaid in spades.

However, there is also reason for Rangers to approach with caution moving forward.

Former Manchester United chief scout Mick Brown told Football Insider last week that Premier League clubs have scouts watching Rangers "weekly" and are sure to be impressed by Naderi.

The ex-recruitment boss outlined that while Rangers are doing everything they can to keep hold of him long-term, that prospect will become increasingly tricky once concrete interest appears.

Former Aberdeen chief executive Keith Wyness told Football Insider on Sunday that Rangers chairman Andrew Cavenagh is "tempted" to personally fund a permanent move for loanee Badredine Bouanani.

The Stuttgart loanee is quickly becoming a fans' favourite at Ibrox, but the option to buy him for £15million feels distant at the moment.

However, Wyness believes that Cavenagh's imminent sale of his £4.5billion-rated company ParetoHealth could potentially see him invest a big chunk into Rangers once again.

The boardroom expert suggested that could be used to fund a permanent move for Bouanani, provided that he continues to impress.

#2096. St Mirren 0 Rangers 2: Winless away run ended with comfortable victory for Ibrox side

Rangers banished their recent away day blues with a solid 2-0 win over St Mirren in Paisley.

Draws against Dundee and Hearts in their last two William Hill Premiership games away from Ibrox had blemished the Gers’ focused title challenge, but Derek McInnes’s side were determined to leave The Marbill Coaches Stadium without a mark on them.

In-form striker Ryan Naderi scored with a soft penalty after 18 minutes before returning skipper Dan Neil added a second just after the hour mark with a deflected strike to extend the Light Blues’ unbeaten run in all competitions to 12 games.

Rangers moved to within one point of leaders Celtic having played the same number of fixtures, albeit the Hoops can can restore their four-point lead against Kilmarnock at Celtic Park on Sunday before the the international break gives the league another breather.

The unusual 8pm kick off on a Saturday night added atmosphere to the evening. St Mirren boss Craig McLeish made five changes, with Declan John, Louis Jackson, Samuel Ramos, Ismeal Kabia and Jake Young all coming in while Neil replaced Tuur Rommens and James Penrice dropped to left-back.

Amid a hurly-burly start to the game, Buddies keeper Jacob Chapman saved an early effort from Rangers wide-man Badredine Bouananai, then in the 12th minute made a crucial block from Naderi, who latched on to a Kevin Kelsy header, at the expense of a corner which came to nothing.

However, the big striker soon made amends.

Back-tracking St Mirren attacker Ramos was far from happy when referee Nick Walsh pointed to the spot following his challenge on Penrice just inside the box, after the Gers defender had raced 60 yards to back up the Light Blues’ South Korea international attacker Kim Min-su.

It looked like there had been little contact but a VAR check confirmed the penalty and Naderi, with a stuttering run up, casually sent Chapman the wrong way with his spot-kick for his ninth goal of the season.

The aggrieved home side fought furiously to get back on level terms and on a counter after 37 minutes, Ramos tested visiting keeper Ivor Pandur with a decent drive from the edge of the box, before Jake Young fired a shot high over the bar.

In a sprightly start to the second half, with Kim showing some delightful touches around the St Mirren penalty area, Kelsy drove wide of the far post from 16 yards.

Then, in the 54th minute, Kim set up Kelsy but Chapman brilliantly deflected the close-range dink and the home side got the ball to safety before the stretching Kelsy could not connect properly with a cross from midfielder Nicolas Raskin.

However, the visitors eventually got the second when another swift attack ended with the ball coming out to Neil, whose shot came off St Mirren defender Louis Jackson and ended up in the back of the net.

St Mirren kept battling and Pandur made a terrific save from substitute Eseosa Sule’s strike from a Declan John cross.

The Rangers keeper then denied another St Mirren replacement, Luke Thomas, before Saints defender Calvin Ramsay headed against the outside of the post from the rebound, and that was effectively the end of St Mirren’ possible comeback.

#2094. Morgan Rogers 'endangered opponent' in 'unacceptable' Chelsea vs Sunderland incident - ex-PGMOL chief

Correspondent AUTHORITY NCTJ-qualified football journalist with experience at VAVEL, Hayters TV, SPORTbible, and Centredevils. FOCUS Premier League analysis, tactical deep-dives, and original opinion content across Arsenal, Chelsea, Tottenham, Manchester City, and Celtic. THE INSIGHT Evan utilises a network of club and industry contacts to deliver verified, high-speed reporting. He provides specialist tactical and analytical content to ensure fans get beyond the headlines and understand the full picture.

Morgan Rogers was fortunate not to see at least a yellow card after catching Trai Hume with his knee as Chelsea lost 1-0 to Sunderland on Sunday.

That is the opinion of former head of PGMOL and FIFA referee, Keith Hackett, speaking exclusively to Football Insider.

Enzo Le Fee's first-half penalty ultimately separated the sides after what was a game packed with controversial decisions.

Sunderland's penalty was heavily disputed after Brian Brobbey looked to have taken hold of Levi Colwill's shirt before the Chelsea defender was penalised.

The Blues felt that they should have had a penalty just minutes before, when Cole Palmer was taken out by Luke O'Nien on the edge of the box.

Rogers has enjoyed a superb start to life at Chelsea since completing the £117million move, but he was perhaps fortunate to complete the 90 minutes on Sunday.

How did Morgan Rogers not get a red card for this? A blatantly obvious knee to the head which VAR reviewed & ticked off?Chelsea have had awful decisions against them in this game but that doesn’t excuse getting away with this weak act. pic.twitter.com/10aZIpI4vU

Chelsea's frustration grew as the second-half went on, with Sunderland holding strong and continuing to dominate much of the action.

Some of those frustrations appeared to boil over when Rogers walked past a downed Hume during a break in play.

The defender was on his haunches when the Chelsea player walked past, knocking his knee into his opponent's head.

Rogers was immediately apologetic, and referee Jarred Gillett did not dish out any punishment.

"This is unacceptable behaviour which is clearly endangering the safety of an opponent," Hackett told Football Insider.

"This should have been brought to the attention of the referee because it certainly required a sanction.

"The minimum sanction should be a yellow card, because of a lack of excessive force."

Interestingly, Rogers and Hume have come to blows before at the Stadium of Light.

Last season, the Sunderland defender launched the then-Aston Villa man into the air with a crunching challenge that did not even draw a foul.

Replays showed that the tackle had certainly been excessive, with the England international unlikely to have forgotten it.

The Black Cats would later post a video of the tackle on social media, drawing a response from Rogers.

"Great message to send out. Dangerous tackles getting highlight reels," he wrote.

#2093. Bayern were ready to pay £58.3m for Rio Ngumoha & may test Liverpool again

Rio Ngumoha’s future at Liverpool could be under threat next summer.

That’s because Bayern Munich reportedly remain ‘in talks’ with the young Englishman’s camp following a failed push to sign the winger this year.

Christian Falk reports for CF Bayern Insider that FC Bayern were prepared to put their money where their mouth is for the teenager in the summer.

A figure to the tune of €70m [£58.3m] was discussed, however, Liverpool’s uncompromising position on the matter meant that an alternative avenue in Ismael Saibari was instead prioritised.

“It is TRUE: Bayern Munich were prepared to pay €70m [£58.3m] for Rio Ngumoha. As we know, Bayern have been searching really hard for options on the left wing,” the head of sport at BILD said.

“We talked about Bradley Barcola, whom they were in contact with, and they were also in contact with Liverpool’s young talent. There were talks, his brother talked with FC Bayern, but it was a difficult situation for Bayern Munich. It was not clear if Liverpool would sell him or not. The price wouldn’t have been extremely high.

“So, you see, the club’s decision-makers feel he’d be a great option for Bayern Munich, which is why Ngumoha is still on Bayern’s shortlist. In the end, they had to decide for Ismael Saibari. Rio would have been complicated, so they just looked to seal the comparatively easier transfer of the two. Bayern are still in talks with Ngumoha’s camp, however, and he could be an option for the summer.”

You’d have to think Andoni Iraola and Co. will be pretty comfortable despite interest from abroad in Ngumoha’s services.

The player’s move to Anfield from Chelsea – which infuriated decision-makers over in the English capital at the time – was prompted by a desire for a clear pathway to the first team and developmental opportunities.

While the minutes are comparatively fewer and further between in the Premier League, the 18-year-old has been repeatedly trusted in Europe, racking up 285 minutes from a possible 360 in the Champions League. With 628 minutes picked up across all competitions in 2026/27, Rio Ngumoha is already well on course to blow last season’s total (1,065) out of the water.

READ MORE: ‘I like him a lot’ – Romelu Lukaku has been mindblown by Liverpool player he could face tonight

The other thing worth bearing in mind is this isn’t a manager throwing the left-sided winger out on the pitch willy-nilly. Andoni Iraola has shown a clear interest in developing Ngumoha into a more well-rounded, positionally versatile winger. After some initial struggles on the right flank, it’s already paying off.

Yes, at FC Bayern, the former Chelsea academy product would likely get plenty of minutes deputising for Luis Diaz in a less intense league, and the attraction of that possibility can’t be understated.

But if the ultimate goal is development and access to a pathway, he’s clearly already got that at Liverpool.

#2092. Furious Aberdeen fans demand Stephen Robinson axe amid miserable form

Stephen Robinson's Aberdeen were booed off the pitch at Pittodrie following their 4-0 hammering at the hands of Hibs.

The visitors arrived at the stadium rock bottom of the Scottish Premiership table having won just two league games all season up until they rocked up at the Granite City.

Dons had been on a bit of a poor run of form themselves and Robinson found himself under pressure even before kick-off with supporters' patience wearing thin.

So when they shipped four against Marink Reedijk's strugglers thanks to goals from Jamie McGrath, Callum Wright, Nicky Cadden and Thibault Klidje, both sides swapped spots in the division.

The boos rung out from within Pittodrie with calls for Robinson to depart becoming louder.

And Chris Sutton, on Sky Sports punditry duties, reckons the former St Mirren head coach may want to "do the honourable thing" by walking away before he's pushed.

"At the start of the season it was all about ‘it’s my team’, it’s a case where it feels the club is too big for him, the job is too big for him,” said Sutton. “Maybe he should do the honourable thing and walk away, but it’ll probably end in the sack.”

Robinson was determined to stick around despite the defeat and insisted he would remain at the helm until he's told otherwise.

#2091. Celtic have an uncomfortable Jota truth, 0% and 17% stats vs Kilmarnock show it

Correspondent AUTHORITY Sports journalist with experience at GamingINTEL and GRV Media; University of Wolverhampton graduate. FOCUS Data content, opinion, and general news coverage across the Breaking Media network. THE INSIGHT Scott utilises a network of club and industry contacts to deliver verified, broad-spectrum reporting. He provides the data and opinion foundations behind the headlines to ensure fans get the full story as it happens.

Jota is a fan favourite at Celtic, stemming from his original spell with the Glasgow side.

The Portuguese winger returned in the winter of 2025, but was then hit by an ACL injury in April of the 2024-25 campaign.

Jota would then be ruled out for 18 months, missing the entirety of last season, with Celtic going on to lift the title.

Now, in the last month, the 27-year-old has returned to action and was handed his first start since 2025 against Kilmarnock.

While Celtic picked up the 1-0 win, there is an unfortunate truth emerging about Jota.

He may not be ready to be a starter for the Glasgow outfit.

There is no doubt that Jota possesses the quality to make a significant difference for Celtic when he is fully fit and firing.

However, his performance against Kilmarnock showed just how much work remains before he can be trusted to deliver consistently at the level expected of him.

As per FotMob, Jota completed zero of his three attempted dribbles against Kilmarnock.

Additionally, he was weak in his duels, winning just one of seven throughout his 45-minute display - a 17 per cent success.

The left-winger also had just two touches in the opposition box, while he was beaten down the wing twice by being dribbled past.

Whether or not the same player Celtic fans have loved is still there remains to be seen.

But that showing against Kilmarnock proved that he may still be a long way off returning to that.

O'Neill cannot afford to hand out sentimental starts, even if supporters want to see him on the pitch.

He has spent a long time on the sidelines, and he is clearly not ready to have an impact to that degree yet.

With the international break now set to get underway, Jota must use this as a chance to improve himself, and potentially get himself ready for a starring role in the future.

#2087. How football fanzines gave supporters a voice and changed the game forever

As has been evident once again during the opening months of the new season, Scottish football fans are not exactly slow to voice their displeasure or shy about agitating for change.

If they are unhappy with how their team is performing on the park or the way their club is being run off it, then they tend to make their feelings known.

Such activism is very much a modern-day phenomenon. So why do rabble-rousers stage protests in the streets, gather in angry mobs outside of stadiums, hold up inflammatory banners in the stands and boycott matches and merchandise when they are aggrieved about a perceived injustice?

Daniel Gray, the English author, editor of Scottish football quarterly Nutmeg and presenter of the When Saturday Comes podcast, believes the fanzine movement which reached its zenith in the 1980s and 1990s altered the landscape of the sport forever and ultimately emboldened the present-day supporter.

Gray’s fascination with fanzines – which can be traced back to the discarded copy of Fly Me To The Moon that he retrieved from the Ayresome Park terraces at a Middlesbrough match as an eight-year-old boy – has led to him penning a fascinating history of the independently produced publications which have long held him in thrall.

Fanzine: The Story of Football’s Alternative Press drives home how much professional football has changed, both for good and for ill, in the past five decades and underlines the role played in that transformation by those who grew frustrated at their voices not being heard during what was unquestionably a dark period in the game.

“Fanzines have led directly to so much of what we see going on in the sport today,” he said. “They were the first time that fans had ever spoken up for themselves. Before that, where and when did you ever hear from supporters?

“Maybe you got the odd letter in the local newspaper from time to time. But that would have been about it. There was never any criticism in the matchday programme. But finding a collective voice paved the way for what came next. It empowered fans.

“There was a definite reaction to fanzines. Clubs, politicians and the police were all terrified about having their authority questioned for the first time. Nobody would think twice about questioning the way the game is run now. There is a lineage back to fanzines in that.

“I am completely in awe of the people who were behind the whole fanzine movement. It would have been very easy for them to sit and moan and do nothing about the state of football in the 1980s. But they did something else altogether.”

Daniel Gray's new book Fanzine (Image: Promotional)

The Shamrock is widely considered to be the first football fanzine in the United Kingdom. It was a short-lived publication which John Doogan, a member of the Shamrock Celtic Supporters Club in Edinburgh, launched in 1963 due to his growing frustration at how poorly the Parkhead club was faring.

It contained poisonous attacks on the board and scathing analysis of the team and players, was sold outside the stadium on matchdays and became, much to the annoyance of the besieged hierarchy, popular due to the widespread disenchantment among the support.

Gray has seen a copy of the first edition which is held in the extensive fanzine archives in the National Library of Scotland in the capital. He is firmly of the opinion it is as important a tome as its prized copy of the Gutenberg Bible. “It is quite something,” he said. “It is up there with all of their ancient relics for me.”

It was, though, a different era that he was most interested in. Fanzine focuses on a turbulent time of seismic change in British football.

“I honed in on the 10-year period between the mid-1980s, when the fanzine boom really started, and the mid-1990s, when modern football, in inverted commas, came into being,” he said.

“I came across research which claimed, and it was a conservative estimate, that a million fanzines were sold in the 1980s and 1990s. It became this mass movement. I wanted to tell the story of that movement, but also to tell the story of that time in football through the eyes of the fans.

“I wanted to show what fans were thinking about and feeling. I knew the conditions fans experienced when they went to a match were bad, but I didn't realise quite how bad until I started to go through those thousands of fanzines. There is a lot of stuff about how fans were treated by the police and how unsafe a lot of the grounds were.

“The public perception of football fans was just so bad. The perception was that all fans were hooligans. Fanzines came about to show that was untrue, to show that a lot of fans were funny and bright and talked about music and politics and books and other things. They really did reshape the way the fans were perceived.”

Gray added, “One of the greatest agonies of going through all of these old fanzines was seeing how prescient many of the writers were. A lot of them were saying grounds were inherently unsafe, a lot of them were warning that bad things were going to happen.

“Sure enough, there were then these big, horrible events, the disasters at Bradford, at Heysel and at Hillsborough. It was far, far worse than anyone could possibly have imagined.

Meadowbank Thistle fanzine AWOL (Image: Promotional)

“So their writing was incredibly perceptive. The quality of the writing, the campaigning and the solidarity between them all helped to change both the way fans were viewed and the conditions in which they watched matches.

“In the mid-1980s, you didn't admit you were a football fan in polite company. By the early 1990s, television networks and radio stations were desperate to have fan-based content. Celebrities, too, were trying to attach themselves to football. A lot changed in a short journey.”

But it was the edgy, often bizarre, frequently hilarious humour in the fanzines which Gray, and so many football supporters of his vintage, adored. He found himself in stitches as he perused the pages of beloved Scottish titles like AWOL, the fabled Meadowbank Thistle publication which is highly prized by collectors.

“I came across an Arbroath fanzine from the late 1980s called Tomato Soup and Lentils in the National Library archives," he said. "It had a bit of the Brechin hedge sellotaped to it. It was a free gift.

“I spoke to Archie MacGregor of the marvellous The Absolute Game and he felt that Scottish fanzines were different from English fanzines and perhaps had more humour in them because fans up here in Scotland weren't faced with as many obstacles as fans in England were. ID cards, for example, were being threatened down south at one point.

“So the tone was slightly different here in Scotland, there was probably a bit more room for sarcasm. They were very sardonic and quite surreal at times. They were far more earnest in England.

“Generally speaking, the lower down the leagues the club was, the better the fanzine it had. There was far more for their fans to moan about so it made for much better content. So the St Mirren and Dundee United fanzines would tend to have a far higher level of sarcasm.

“Meadowbank Thistle had a strangely large number of fanzines for such a small club. AWOL was utterly fantastic. It is loved by a lot of people. There was some football content, but on the whole they wrote about other things.

“They once had an article that was headlined 'The Shoplifter’s Guide to Edinburgh'. That was a bit too much for the club and those responsible got hauled in to answer some questions. But that was fairly typical of the strand of Scottish humour that ran through fanzines. There was definitely surrealism.”

The origin stories of the titles, which include Brian Moore's Head Looks Uncannily Like London Planetarium (Gillingham), The Deranged Ferret (Lincoln City), The Memoirs of Seth Bottomley (Port Vale) and 53 Miles West of Venus (Preston North End), were often as funny as the stories contained within.

A fanzine seller at Turf Moor (Image: Phil Oldham / Shutterstock)

Gray particularly liked Wendy Who?, which St Johnstone fans named after a song they regularly belted out during matches at their old Muirton Park home.

"Oh Wendy Saints, oh Wendy Saints, oh Wendy Saints go marching in . . . "

“I loved a Dundee United fanzine called Can I Bring My Dog?," said Gray. "It was a question a United fan asked the organiser of a supporters' bus before a trip to Denmark for a European game. I thought that was brilliant.

“There’s A Store Where the Creatures Meet was a St Mirren fanzine which the author Christopher Brookmyre wrote for. Those are the lyrics from The Doors’ song Love Street, which was obviously the name of their old ground.

“The crossover between music magazines and football fanzines was huge. Quite often when I was going through old fanzines a flexi-disc would fall out."

Gray continued, “Very creative people got involved during what was a really energising time in football. There was an awful lot of quality writing, including by people like Christopher Brookmyre, Irvine Welsh and Neil Forsyth.

“The first time Neil saw his words in print was in a Dundee United fanzine. Irvine wrote for Hibs fanzines under various pseudonyms. He probably cut his teeth writing for Hibs Monthly in the late 1980s. Anyone could send something in. There was a wonderful democracy to it.”

Internet message boards, social media websites and short-form video platforms are the outlets which football supporters use to vent their spleens in 2026. The digital age, though, has by no means brought about an end to fanzines. Indeed, Gray found they are enjoying something of a revival.

“There are around 70 printed fanzines still left,” he said. “A lot of them are old titles like Fly Me To The Moon at Middlesbrough, A Love Supreme at Sunderland and The City Gent at Bradford. But there are new fanzines which younger supporters are producing as well.

“I am sensing a real desire to get away from screens and to embrace this very old medium. I think football supporters love having something ephemeral. They love an object that marks them being at a match.

“Few clubs use physical tickets now and fewer clubs are producing matchday programmes now. So maybe fanzines are becoming your souvenir of the day, of the game.

“It has been a bit unexpected, but it is happening. I see a real interest in getting away from the anger and the hot air of YouTube channels, social media sites and radio phone-ins and a desire to just be a bit more reflective.

A Manchester United fanzine seller at Old Trafford (Image: Philip Oldham/BPI / Shutterstock)

“I don't think there's going to be a full-scale renaissance or a return to what the movement once was. It is similar to the rise in popularity of vinyl records among music lovers, which nobody saw coming. I do feel there is a space for them, a role for them.

“I certainly yearn for the fanzine, for the content that was in them and for the tone of them. So much football writing now is about tactics and transfers. I miss something that is barely relevant to the match I was at, that is full of humour and that reflects what fans actually talk about when they stand behind the goal.

“Yes, the 1980s was undoubtedly a horrific time to watch football. But there were elements to it, like the affordability that went out the window, in the Premier League anyway, when all-seater stadiums came in during the early 1990s, that I do miss.”

Fanzine was a real labour of love for Gray and it shows. It is a forensically detailed, beautifully crafted, utterly engrossing account of the glorious heyday of the often bonkers but invariably brilliant magazines which football fanatics who were determined to have their say produced in their bedrooms, in their garden sheds and on their kitchen tables.

There is, with Scottish magazines like Cappielow Bugle (Morton), Follow Follow (Rangers), Northern Light (Aberdeen), Not The View (Celtic), Railway Ender (Ayr United) and Walking Down The Halbeath Road (Dunfermline) covered, plenty of interest for fans from these shores.

“It was a privilege to write it,” he said. “The sort of person who started a fanzine wasn't really in it for an ego trip or to further their career. Sometimes it takes an outsider like me to say, ‘What you did was incredible’.”

Fanzine: The Story of Football’s Alternative Press by Daniel Gray is published by Bloomsbury Sport, costs £20, and is available to buy now.

#2086. Why under-rated Nico Elvedi is Leeds United's best summer signing

Senior Correspondent AUTHORITY Sports journalist with experience at Football League World and Burton Albion FC; Derby University graduate. FOCUS Transfer coverage and behind-the-scenes insight across the Premier League, EFL, and SPFL. THE INSIGHT Evan utilises a network of club and industry contacts to deliver verified, high-speed transfer reporting. He provides the depth behind the deals to ensure fans get the full story as it happens.

Leeds United centre-back Tarik Muharemovic has received plenty of plaudits of late, but his defensive partner Nico Elvedi has arguably been a better acquisition.

Both stars arrived at Elland Road in the summer as part of the Whites' bid to revamp their defence and add more proven top-level quality to their backline.

Muharemovic joined from Sassuolo in a £34million deal, and already looks likely to be a player who Leeds can secure a significant profit on in future.

The Bosnian gem has attracted plenty of attention for his displays so far, and that has taken the limelight away from Elvedi, who has arguably been equally as impressive.

The former Borussia Monchengladbach man was someone who Leeds spent several years chasing, and it is now clear while Daniel Farke fought so valiantly to land him.

Elvedi is a veteran of the Bundesliga, but has transitioned admirably into the style of the Premier League, and deserves more attention than he has been getting of late.

Were it not for Muharemovic's early success at Elland Road, the move to bring in Elvedi would be lauded across the Premier League right now.

The Whites secured his services for just £8.5m, as they snapped him up one year before his contract with Monchengladbach was due to expire.

Elvedi boasts over 300 Bundesliga appearances to his name, alongside Champions League experience, and he has shown that with his quality of performances so far.

Throw in the fact that he's been a key part of the Switzerland national team across six international tournaments, and he was always likely to be a success in the Premier League.

He has already won the trust of Farke, who views him as one of the first names on the teamsheet right now.

Muharemovic is rightly getting plenty of credit, but the move to bring in Elvedi has arguably been equally as important for Leeds.

Football Insider revealed on Sunday that centre-back Jaka Bijol could potentially be heading towards the exit door at Elland Road next summer.

Leeds have had a very settled backline so far this season, and the Slovenian has found himself down the pecking order, despite impressing last term.

Sources say that Joe Rodon's return from injury has cast further doubt over Bijol's future, with the Welshman also a trusted figure for Farke.

Bijol was one of Leeds' most impressive performers throughout last season, but his time with the club could soon draw to a close.

#2085. Derek McInnes says 'gallus' Naderi is becoming a striker opponents hate facing

Derek McInnes reckons "gallus" Rangers striker Ryan Naderi is developing into a striker opponents will hate facing.

Naderi impressed in Gers' 2-0 victory over St Mirren, earning glowing praise from his boss, who believes the Czech Republic international is beginning to show exactly what it takes to lead the line at Ibrox.

The manager wants his striker to develop a reputation for being a real handful, insisting a bit of attitude is essential when leading the attack.

He said: "He needs to build that reputation for being horrible to play against. You need your number nine to be a bit gallus and have himself up there.

"You cannae be unsure, you cannae be, 'Do I belong here?' I think he's totally shown that he's somebody you can depend on, somebody that can be trusted."

McInnes was particularly impressed with Naderi's willingness to unsettle defenders, run the channels and make his presence felt.

He added: "I thought he ran the gaps, he made sure every one of their centre-backs knew he was there, which is very important.

"At a club like Rangers you're going to get judged on the goals.

"If you're going to lead the line for us, then getting those goals is so important and thankfully with his stats he's really contributing."

Naderi now heads away with the Czechia, with McInnes believing his international experience has helped him take a significant step forward.

And the Light Blues' boss reckons the supporters are already appreciating the striker's all-action approach.

He said: "Supporters love players who chase lost causes, who run until they're empty really. The fact that he's scoring goals just helps matters with that."

#2084. Darren Beckford remembered after former Hearts striker dies aged 59

Former Heart of Midlothian forward Darren Beckford has sadly passed away at the age of 59.

Beckford enjoyed a brief spell in Gorgie between August and December 1996, making 12 competitive appearances and scoring twice for the Jambos.

The most memorable of those goals was the opener against Dundee in the League Cup semi-final at Easter Road.

Beckford began his professional career with Manchester City before becoming a firm favourite during a memorable spell at Port Vale, where he established himself as a prolific goalscorer.

His well-travelled career also included spells with Norwich City and Preston North End before his short stint in the capital with Hearts.

The striker arrived at Tynecastle during Jim Jefferies' time in charge, joining a Hearts side that would go on to enjoy a memorable period in the late 1990s.

His stay in Edinburgh proved short-lived, but Beckford still managed to make his mark during his few months in maroon, with his League Cup semi-final strike among the highlights.

It was at Port Vale, however, where the forward enjoyed some of the most memorable years of his career and became a popular figure with supporters.

Beckford's passing will be mourned by fans of the many clubs he represented during a career that took him across English and Scottish football.

And his passing has been mourned by former clubs and colleagues across British football,

However, the DR Congo youth international proved his worth with an exceptional showcase for the Northern English side.

And following the international break, he must be a regular in the side to help Sunderland stave off relegation.

Ahoka delivered a performance that should give Le Bris plenty to think about when deciding his midfield options.
