#2032. Glasgow biotech teams up with Nottingham Forest to trial injury risk blood test

A Glasgow biotech company has teamed up with Premier League club Nottingham Forest to investigate whether blood tests could help identify injury risks in professional footballers before they happen.

Entourage, based at Kelvin Campus, is conducting a 12-week study involving the club’s 25-player men’s B team, with support from Scottish Enterprise.

The Entourage Team. (Image: Martin Shields)

The research will use plasma proteomics, the analysis of proteins in blood, to monitor players’ biological responses to training, matches and recovery.

Players will provide blood samples twice a week, allowing researchers to analyse thousands of proteins and track individual responses to physical demands, injuries and recovery.

By combining the results with existing training, workload and clinical information, the team hopes to identify protein patterns that could indicate a greater risk of non-contact soft tissue injuries.

The trial is described as the first high-frequency plasma proteomic study involving a professional sports team.

A blood sample being collected. (Image: Supplied)

The research comes amid concerns about the impact of hamstring injuries in elite football. UEFA figures for the 2021/22 season found they accounted for one in five days of injury absence across elite European football, double the rate recorded two decades earlier.

Entourage’s technology focuses on using protein analysis to better understand inflammation, immune function and recovery. The company is also building a reference dataset for elite athletes, supported by its research centre at Kelvin Campus.

The findings could help clubs develop more personalised training and recovery plans based on players’ individual biological responses.

The company also sees potential applications for its technology beyond sport, including the early detection of conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes and Alzheimer’s.

Entourage lab technician Matthew Mitchell prepares a blood sample for testing in their lab. (Image: Elaine Livingstone)

Entourage was co-founded by Professor Patrick Gunning, Dr Taleb Sedghi and Dr Mark Lindsay and launched with a $5 million pre-seed funding round.

Professor Gunning previously co-founded Dunad Therapeutics and helped secure a $1.3 billion partnership with Novartis.

The company plans to report its findings to Nottingham Forest at the end of the 12-week study.

Voluntary Health Scotland relaunches as Health Creation Scotland to tackle inequality

Century-old foundation stone restored and relocated at Aberdeen children's hospital

Aberdeen 'set' to sack Stephen Robinson as axe looms at Pittodrie

Professor Patrick Gunning, chief executive and co-founder of Entourage, said:"One of the questions we are trying to answer is whether there are signals in the blood that could indicate an increased risk of a non-contact injury.

"That is something we need to investigate through the study."

Dimitrios Kalogiannidis, head of medical at Nottingham Forest, said: "We are deeply committed to evidence-led player care.

"We believe in the importance of building a more robust biological profile of each player, so we’re pleased to be taking part in this research study that could benefit Nottingham Forest and the wider game for years to come."

Entourage’s chief executive and co-founder, Professor Patrick Gunning pictured with lab scientist Daniel Poloske. (Image: Elaine Livingstone)

Dr Mark Lindsay, co-founder of Entourage, said: "We're moving soft-tissue care from estimation to measurement.

"We read the biology of the injury, precision directives guide every stage of treatment, and return to play is decided by the data.

"You can't manage what you can't measure."

#2031. Robinson on the brink but Aberdeen’s deep-rooted problems go far beyond the manager

Friday marked the 40th anniversary of Alex Ferguson quitting Aberdeen for Manchester United, leaving faces like granite behind him.

Media outlets wheeled out old, grainy footage from the day of mourning, as BBC cameras conveyed the lunchtime grief of shell-shocked boozers in King Street’s Pittodrie Bar.

One old boy in a flat cap condemned the lack of loyalty from a man who demanded absolute fidelity from his players. Another proffered the view that Fergie would regret a sudden rush of blood to the head. The fan who felt the move might present Aberdeen with a bit of a problem was a master of understatement.

Four decades since they lost their Napoleon, Aberdeen are a club haunted by the past. Battlefield generals like Ferguson and Willie Miller set the bar so high, those who followed were guaranteed to shoot themselves in the feet.

Read more: Haissem Hassan Celtic absence explained as ‘manoeuvring’ costs winger

The club’s last league title came in May 1985. Major trophies have been as rare as snow in April.

While no one has any expectation of European glory these days, supporters reared on tales of the halcyon days are entitled to expect more than three finishes in the bottom six of the SPFL Premiership since 2021/22.  With a staff cost base of around £16million a year, that’s a scandalous state of affairs.

Had the Beeb returned to the Pittodrie Bar after Saturday’s 4-0 hammering from Hibs, they would have found a support happy to see the latest Aberdeen manager off the premises. Had Stephen Robinson been up for a move to Manchester, they’d have revved the car and driven him south themselves.

When the Northern Irishman leaves, it won’t be by choice. It never is these days.

Under contract until 2029, managerial pay-offs have become an expensive annual event.

And, for the Dons hierarchy, it might now be time to time ask themselves an awkward question. What if all those sacked bosses were never really the problem?

In the last five years, Derek McInnes, Stephen Glass, Jim Goodwin, Barry Robson and Jimmy Thelin all left with a black bin bag tucked under their arm. Robinson will be next to collect his P45 after a hideous second-half collapse against Hibs.

The Aberdeen job is now a poisoned chalice. Hiring managers who have done well elsewhere, the club chews them up, spits them out, then watches on as they move somewhere else and remind everyone that they were never a bad boss in the first place.

McInnes came to within minutes of a league title at Hearts last season and is now breathing down the necks of Celtic as manager of Rangers.

While Glass was always an odd, left-field choice, he had a useful two years at USL Championship side Memphis 901 and was last seen serving as Robbie Keane’s assistant at Ferencvaros.

Goodwin recovered from an ignominious Scottish Cup calamity in Darvel to prove himself a better manager than he looked the day he walked across the Easter Road pitch with a man bag over his shoulder after a 6-0 defeat to Hibs. Dundee United are now a club five places and six points better off than Aberdeen.

Cork City were promoted to the League of Ireland Premier Division last month, earning Barry Robson a new two-year contract in the process.

Two years ago this week, Jimmy Thelin had Aberdeen joint-top of the Premiership after 11 games of the 2024/25 season. Since then, the team have played 77 league games and won 19. That’s a win rate of just 25 per cent.

Supporters never really wanted Robinson in the first place. The people running the club never seemed sold on him either.

The plan was to make an overseas appointment, with Eirik Horneland the preferred candidate in March. When talks with the Norwegian stalled, Sandro Schwarz flew in to watch a game against Celtic, took one look and decided he was better off moving to Moscow.

A solid operator at Motherwell and St Mirren, Robinson was the last man standing at the bar.

Portrayed – harshly – as a long-ball, survival specialist, there was always a question over his ability to win hearts and minds at Aberdeen. To convince the critics he had to hit the ground running and, despite scratching a win over Hearts, that didn’t happen.

A thumping 4-0 win in Motherwell in September proved a false dawn when stats showed that the Dons converted all four of their shots on target and enjoyed possession of just 31 per cent.

Since Fir Park, they have won just once in seven games, against St Mirren. And the Northern Irishman’s demeanour has grown progressively more pained. Weekly monologues on the need to be better have lost any impact.

The first big decision for new chief executive Adrian Bevington, there is a grim inevitability to how this ends and wherever he turns up next, Robinson will do what so many former Aberdeen managers do by displaying a talent for winning games of football at another club. As with so many before, it won’t happen in the Granite City.

A club which sucks the life from promising careers, an Aberdeen manager is only ever two bad games from the sack. The man in the technical area works in a culture of fear, fulfilling the role of human shield for senior figures wary of sticking their head over the parapet.

Non-executive chairman Dave Cormack is a passionate fan in the boardroom. After open-heart surgery three years ago, he tried to take a step back by appointing a chief executive to run the show. Alan Burrows has now gone and every Aberdeen departure – for there are many – turns the finger of accusation turn in Cormack’s direction.

No one can accuse the chairman of failing to back his managers. The Dons have spent substantial sums building, then rebuilding, failing teams. How much they spend is less of a problem than how they spend it.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel was hired to bring strategic and continental know-how. And, at first, the German seemed keen to make himself the centre of attention.

Last season, he was parked beside interim boss Peter Leven in the dugout. These days, you could stand on the Beach Boulevard with a set of strong binoculars and struggle to find his dot on the North Sea horizon.

In Scottish football there is a new unwritten rule. Hearts and Aberdeen, it seems, can never be successful in the same season and, while the Tynecastle club have established themselves as the third force in Scottish football – Falkirk not withstanding – Aberdeen labour in the relegation play-off place.

When Robinson goes, expect the next guy to be an overseas appointment. A blameless optimist who vaguely remembers Aberdeen winning a European trophy in the days when he was knee-high to a grasshopper, and sees a club which can – and should – be so much more than the blazing bin fire it is now.

#2021. GdS: A ‘true disaster’ – scrutiny intensifies as Milan sink to new low in Ferencvaros loss

AC Milan fell to a third Europa League defeat in four games last night at San Siro, losing against Ferencvaros who maintained their perfect start.

La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) begin a report by asking the obvious question: what is the real Milan? Is it the aggressive, focused and at times dazzling side seen in the derby at the weekend, or the listless, disjointed, and sterile team witnessed yesterday against Ferencváros?

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In all likelihood, the real Milan are both – doomed, partly due to structural limitations, to oscillate between positive performances and lacklustre displays. To be clear, the Rossoneri won’t get far in any competition this way, as there can be no ambition without consistency.

Their last six matches have been a constant see-saw between victory and defeat. On only one of five occasions have Milan managed to come back from a deficit, a sign of a profound struggle to react.

Yesterday, their Europa League campaign became dangerously complicated: direct qualification for the next stage is now little more than a pipe dream, and even reaching the play-offs is hanging in the balance.

As things stand, Milan would be eliminated, and the schedule includes a daunting away trip to face Olympiacos and a home match against Sunderland, followed by two theoretically easier fixtures. The ‘Version A’ of Milan would have no trouble finishing in the top 24, but ‘Version B’ risks falling short.

One must also ask how much they truly care about the Europa League. While it is true that the squad lacks depth and injuries provide a valid excuse, Amorim’s team selections made it clear that Sunday’s away match in Genoa was considered the higher priority.

Yet, making such choices hinders growth. So far in Europe, the Diavolo have delivered three embarrassing performances in four games in Europe. It is a hard pill to swallow, but this is Milan: an international competition cannot be treated like a midweek friendly.

The match against a very good Ferencváros side was handled poorly: a terrible approach, an overly convoluted tactical set-up (even accounting for absences, which must be considered but do not justify such absolute mediocrity), and a complete lack of intensity.

It was as if the players were still suffering from a hangover following their derby celebrations. Amorim opted for a 4-2-3-1 formation, tasking Jashari with orchestrating play, while relying on the pace of Hutchinson and Cissé to disrupt the disciplined Hungarian defence.

The problem, however, was that there was no bow from which to launch those arrows. Jashari once again displayed a concerning lack of personality. Borbely assigned Bero to mark him, and that move alone was enough to reduce the Swiss player to performing only the most basic tasks, which he executed poorly.

Another issue in the build-up phase was the advanced positioning of Rabiot, who was drawn too far toward the final third, making him easy to shield. Unlike in the derby, he found himself receiving the ball with his back to the goal, almost always forcing him to pass backward.

Rabiot’s true value lies in his box-to-box quality: mobility is essential to maximizing his strengths, yet yesterday he was effectively caged by Amorim’s tactical design. Then there is Ramos, who touched the ball just three times (yes, three) in 30 minutes, despite the team holding 68% possession.

What is the point of maintaining possession if your best player remains on the periphery of the match and your centre-forward is never provided with a service? It was fortunate for Milan that, in the first half, Joseph displayed the worst of his repertoire, squandering two prime opportunities.

Realising the issues, Amorim tried to jolt the team into life by bringing on indispensable starters (Pulisic, Moreira and Gila) and dropping Rabiot deeper. It yielded no positive results, as the team’s build-up play remained predictable and their defense lacked cohesion.

Joseph made amends for his first-half finishing errors by scoring twice into an empty net. The first goal was gifted by a reckless back-pass from De Winter that Torriani failed to control; the second coming on a counter-attack, set up by an intelligent touch from Zachariassen.

Meanwhile, Milan’s first shot on target didn’t arrive until the 36th minute of the second half, courtesy of Hutchinson. By that point Ferencváros were down to ten men following Yusuf’s sending-off, and Amorim had deployed both Modrić and Camarda.

The coach opted for an improbable 4-2-4 formation with Moreira playing as a left-back. It was a move born of resignation, or rather, desperation. Which version of Milan will show up at Marassi on Sunday? It’s a question that naturally piques one’s curiosity.

#2020. 'At fault' .. 'quite sloppy' .. 'very few touches' - ratings from Crawley Town's embarrassing loss to Wimborne Town

Seung-Woo Yang gave Wimborne the lead with a magical finish ten minutes into the game.

Crawley dominated possession but failed to test the Wimborne keeper, with a lack of creativity and attacking impetus letting them down.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The Reds looked to be building some momentum early in the second half but that soon faded.

With ten minutes remaining Cam Munn tapped it home to make it 2-0 – the win putting the Magpies into the second round and giving the Wimborne a day they will never forget and Crawley one they will want to in a hurry.

Here are our player ratings – and the fact the man we picked out as Crawley’s best operator wasn’t even on the pitch in the first half says it all…

Vito Mannone: 3.5 – The experienced goalkeeper was at fault for Wimborne’s opener in the first half as his throw fell short of its target and the home side capitalised. Did produce a good save while Wimborne led 2-0.

Kellan Gordon: 3 – Drove down the right hand side well at times and got into good crossing positions but his deliveries failed to beat the first man on a number of occasions or were too close to the keeper.

Charlie Barker: 4 – The 23 year old was in midfield once again and battled well at times winning some of his aerial duels but was quite sloppy on the ball throughout the game.

Priestley Farquharson: 5 – One of the Reds’ stronger players in what was an embarrassing performance. Won most of his duels and used his strength and physicality well during the first half. He had to come off with an injury midway through the second 45.

Danilo Orsi: 3 – Crawley opted to play direct particularly in the first half and the striker struggled to make any impact at all having very few touches before being taken off at half time.

Stephen Duke-McKenna: 4 – Had very little joy down the right hand side and rarely got the rub of the green with the solidity of the Wimborne backline.

Lewis Richards: 3.5 – Quiet first half from the left back. Didn’t offer anything from an attacking front to drive Crawley forward let alone defensively.

Jonny Russell: 4.5 – The Irishman was a left centre-back again and definitely improved in the second half with some good runs from deep.

Jude Arthurs: 4 – Former Bromley midfielder struggled to galvanise his teammates as Crawley captain and wasn’t really involved in the build-up as the Reds looked to play it long, struggling to play through the 7th tier side.

Dylan Morgan: 5 – Just like Duke-McKenna, didn’t have a lot of luck down his flank on the left. Had a few shots fired wide and his crosses did not lead to anything prosperous.

Kai Jennings: 3 – The Wimbledon loanee had a tough time in midfield but did have a good effort in the first half while it was 1-0 which flashed wide.

Josh Flint: 6 – Gave the Reds some momentum when he came on at half-time, driving his team up the pitch with his marauding runs and was by far Crawley’s best player.

Nathan Tinsdale: 4 – The youngster struggled in difficult circumstances like many of his teammates.

Pemi Aderoju: 4 – Was more effective up front than Orsi, winning flick ons from the lofted balls up front. Had one great chance five minutes into the second half which he volleyed straight at the keeper.

Ben Heneghan: 3.5 – The 6ft 3 centre back came on to make his debut but failed to make any sort of impact.

Malcolm Ebiowei: 5 – A few neat touches and dribbles from Derby County attacker but didn’t have enough time to effect the game.

#2016. Hutchinson worryingly claims ‘a lot’ of Milan players ‘didn’t show that hunger’ in Ferencvaros loss

Omari Hutchinson has questioned the desire of some of the players in the AC Milan squad who are not playing regularly.

Milan sunk to perhaps their lowest point of Ruben Amorim’s tenure so far as they were beaten 2-0 by Ferencvaros. The away side were good value for the win, and it complicates the mission to get into the knockout stages of the Europa League given the current position outside the top 24.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Amorim did not hold back after the game, accusing his team of lacking heart and desire. It is a third defeat in four European games for the Rossoneri, which is far off the expectations of one of the supposed pre-tournament favourites.

Hutchinson was interviewed by CBS Sports Golazo at the end of last night’s game and he offered his thoughts on what was another rough night, with MilanNews relaying his words.

“I think we had a very slow start. I think we were mentally prepared: they showed us all the tactics, what we had to do and how to start.

“I think we’ve been having a lot of slow starts lately, and even though we came out with a slightly more positive attitude in the second half, today it just wasn’t enough.

“I don’t think we showed that hunger to get to the ball, to make an impact in front of goal. So yeah, it was all very, very slow.”

And what needs to be done in the next matches to improve your performance and your style of play?

“I just think we need to play like we did against Inter. You could feel the energy in the locker room; you could tell we wanted to win. I think we didn’t show much humility today.

“We didn’t want to… well, a lot of players who aren’t playing didn’t show that hunger to want a starting spot, and I think that wasn’t enough. I think we’ll have to start strong on Sunday and be really good with the ball.”

Will you be able to find the strength to climb the rankings?

“Yes, yes, I think the game isn’t over until we’re out, so we just have to keep focusing. Yes, we just have to improve. We have a good group, the staff always helps us, shows us what we have to do.

“And now I think it’s up to us. I think we let everyone down today and we have another game on Sunday, we have to focus on that and come out strong.”

#2015. Everything we’ve done in training was for nothing – Blackwell embarrassed at Crawley Town’s Cup loss at Wimborne

The Reds slipped to a new low as they were outplayed by seventh tier Wimborne Town, who beat them 2-0 in the FA Cup first round – and it was the second straight season Cralwey had gone out at this stage to a non-league side.

Goals from Seung-woo Yang and Cameron Munn secured the deserved win for the hosts, as Crawley were played off the park.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Speaking with club media after the game, interim manager Blackwell said he was ‘embarrassed’. He added: “I’m not very happy with what I’ve seen today, and I’ve learnt a lot today. This was a key game for me because expectation was on the players. I wanted to see how they would react with expectations. And I’m sorry to say I’ve not been impressed with what I’ve seen today.”

The Reds came into this game after good results against Tranmere and Oldham – and were long favourites to proceed to the next round.

Crawley fans travelled in their numbers but left disappointed and deeply unhappy at the performance. Blackwell said “I’ve got to apologise to the Crawley fans. And there were some here and there’s some not very happy fans. And quite right, I wouldn’t be happy.

“This has been a really interesting two weeks since I’ve been here. And what I’m concerned about is the undulation in the performances. That, for me, isn’t good. I’ve told everybody where the club is. They know where it is. And while I’m here, I’ll work my socks off for the club. That’s what I’ll do.

“But the players have got to have a long hard look at themselves. They’ve got to decide whether they want to be playing at clubs like this next year or in the Football League. It’s a simple equation. They’ve got to know and have that desire for me to be professional footballers and want to be in the Football League. It’s as simple as that. It’s not hard to work that out.”

Blackwell had mentioned in his pre-match preview about paying the utmost respect to the opposition, but he didn’t feel they did. When asked about that, he said “No I didn’t. I said to the players if I started, I’d still be there at 10 o’clock tonight. All the things that we’ve tried to do and everything we’ve done in training; everything was for nothing.

“If you can’t follow the plans and you can’t follow the roles and responsibilities and you duck out of physical challenges… they were a team that were physical, we knew that. We didn’t need to fight them. We just needed to play some football. We didn’t do any of it. So, I’m bitterly disappointed with what I’ve seen.”

Crawley’s next fixture is against Brentford U21s in the Jersey Mikes’ Trophy on Tuesday (Nov 10) then nothing until Saturday, November 21, when they take on Fleetwood Town at home, which gives Blackwell some time to get the side’s confidence back up.

He said “We saw a good performance against Tranmere and could have won it. We went to Oldham and won it. Then I see this today. So, I don’t know what I’m going to get in the next game.

“And as a manager or as a coach, it’s a nightmare when you don’t know what the performance level your team’s going to give you. I need consistency in performances. We need consistency as a club. That isn’t consistent, so I’ve got to work out what we can do with it.”

#2013. Leeds United 1 Tottenham 0: Personality counts as Daniel Farke has everything that Roberto de Zerbi doesn't possess

Organisation, obduracy. Watching each other’s backs and sticking together.

Strong minds, intensity and feeding off the five-star fuel which is in abundant supply when Leeds attack the Gelderd End, particularly in the second half of matches.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

More especially when those present sense that one of the so called ‘name’ clubs don’t particularly fancy it on a November day in Yorkshire.

It was a win for the home dressing room and the culture that Farke has carefully constructed. He knew it - unity and commitment were the first two words he used to describe his side’s first victory in six games - and his Spurs counterpart Roberto De Zerbi also knew it too.

These are the sort of wins that proper managers love. Ones that are hewn from a bit of adversity. Conversely, they constitute defeats that tell a lot to the vanquished.

De Zerbi said that his side lacked ‘personality’ in the second half and he was spot-on. Personality counts in tight matches.

And while Noah Okafor may have only been on the pitch for just over a minute and a half before his match-winning strike 11 minutes from the end of normal time, nobody could say that the hosts’ breakthrough wasn’t coming or deserved.

Yes, Spurs were entitled to feel hard done by what happened - or didn’t - in the 37th minute with Mathys Tel. Ultimately that wasn’t the point.

A lengthy VAR check scrutinised Jayden Bogle’s challenge on the Spurs man close to the near touchline. The Leeds defender’s left-boot raked the back of Tel’s Achilles, leaving the Frenchman writhing in agony for a short while. Briefly, he did manage to continue before succumbing. Tel left Elland Road in a protective boot and on crutches.

In a post on X, the Premier League Match Centre later confirmed Bogle’s action was viewed as accidental and at low speed. It spared him from a red card, despite seemingly setting a precedent, as similar recent challenges from Jean-Phillipe Mateta and Ryan Sessegnon were deemed sending-off offences.

Spurs submitted a subsequent complaint to Pro Ref following the latest incident. But it was not the reason why they lost. Saturday served as a reminder that when things don’t go in the direction that you like, you show character and crack on.

In the second half, a group of players - several brought in at considerable expense in the summer - lacked cojones, as the Spanish say.

De Zerbi might be Italian, but he wouldn’t need to be told what it meant. He is still finding out about his group as a collective. Farke knows everything about his own and implicitly trusts them.

His Leeds side weren’t bad in the first half, but they weren’t particularly good either. Spurs possessed more of the poise on show. Mateus Fernandes - rightly cleared of a handball offence by an early VAR check - was prominent.

Seeking a fourth successive Premier League win for the first time in over 1,000 days, the visitors laid a decent platform without forging a lead in the opening half.

The second half was a different story. Leeds’ senior professionals in the likes of Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Ethan Ampadu took over.

Their eyes lit up and sensed Spurs uncertainty, while the unforgiving Leeds crowd reminded the visitors of their location south of the Watford Gap. Soft was the polite word employed.

Unlike those in white, the ones in indigo couldn't get going. Leeds, for whom Melvin Bard made an excellent impression after coming on for Gabriel Gudmundsson (hamstring) starred to become incessant in a half when they posted 13 goal attempts.

Nico Elvedi headed a rebound wide after Calvert-Lewin caused consternation. Ao Tanaka spurned a terrific chance, while Antonin Kinsky later made a splendid reaction save to tip over a hooked effort from the recalled Sean Longstaff.

De Zerbi had made a treble change to try and change the narrative. Farke played the telling cards.

Bard's throw-in on the left was flicked on by Calvert-Lewin. Replacement Harry Wilson challenged Rodrigo Bentancur and the ball dropped invitingly for Okafor, who did the rest. On the pitch for just 97 seconds, it was the quickest goal by a top-flight substitute this season.

The number for Spurs to mull over was 51 - the amount of Premier League games in which they have failed to win after going behind.

The late onslaught never came, although James Trafford made one key late save to deny Jan Paul van Hecke. After Bournemouth, that was important.

Leeds United: Trafford; Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic; Bogle (Rodon 93), Ampadu, Longstaff (Greuv 93), Tanaka (Wilson 77), Gudmundsson (Bard HT); Nmecha (Okafor 77), Calvert-Lewin. Substitutes unused: Zetterer, James, Aaronson, Bijol.

Tottenham Hotspur: Kinsky; Porro (Gallagher 65), Van Hecke, Van der Ven, Robertson; Tonali, Fernandes (Bentacur 65), Gray; Kudus (Williams-Barnett 83), Tel (Solanke 43); Marmoush (Kulusevski 65). Substitutes unused: Gunter, Senesi, Maddison, Davies.

#2012. Steve Herbert: Just when we thought it couldn't get any worse, Crawley Town hit a new low

The most embarrassing performance and result since we became a football league club in 2011.

As a football club we have hit a new low, when we already thought sitting bottom of the entire football league couldn’t get any worse, we end up being out fought and outplayed by a team who plays at the same level as Three Bridges.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Let that sink in for a minute… a team who plays in a stadium not much different to Jubilee Field has just knocked us out of the FA Cup first round in front of a national television audience.

Losing last season at Boreham Wood at the same stage was bad, but this is next level stuff.

Only this club could produce a result like this one. Four hundred and seventy six Reds fans gave up a whole Remembrance Sunday to attend this horror show in Dorset. Wimborne is probably one of the trickiest places to get too, especially by public transport. It’s quicker to get to Manchester and Liverpool by train than it is to get to the South West. Yet we take the largest away following of the season, and the players let us down like that. Absolutely disgusting.

After talking up all the positivity of the last two league results against Tranmere & Oldham, it’s such a shame that the team have let Kevin Blackwell down so spectacularly. All I can say is thank god the Rotherham game has been postponed. At least it saves us another wasteful day out.

Where do we go from here? Who knows. All I know is if I was one of those players who have let the club down massively and embarrassed every fan who attended and those that watched at home, then a reaction needs to be seen at home to Fleetwood Town in the shape of a performance and a win.

#2011. Aberdeen 'set' to sack Stephen Robinson as axe looms at Pittodrie

Aberdeen look set to sack boss Stephen Robinson within the next 24 hours.

The 51-year-old is on the brink just eight months into his Pittodrie reign following a dismal start to the campaign.

Saturday’s bruising 4-0 defeat to Hibs has piled further pressure on Robinson, with the Dons languishing in 11th place in the Premiership after managing just three league wins all season.

According to the Scottish Sun, Dons supremo Dave Cormack is poised to convene a crunch board meeting, with Robinson facing the axe barring a dramatic late reprieve.

Robinson replaced Jimmy Thelin in March and worked alongside sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel during a summer of major change at Pittodrie.

Furious Aberdeen fans turned on the manager with chants of “sacked in the morning” following the Hibs hammering, and Cormack now looks set to give them their wish.

Read more: Haissem Hassan Celtic absence explained as ‘manoeuvring’ costs winger

Robinson was made to sweat yesterday as the Dons board stopped short of making a swift decision on his future.

But barring an unlikely last-gasp reprieve, new chief executive Adrian Bevington looks set to be handed the task of identifying the club’s next boss over the international break.

Robinson is braced for bad news but remained defiant after the heavy loss.

He said: “I’ve got belief in my ability. You don’t have 500 games as a manager if you don’t.

“It’s a difficult situation, difficult at the moment for myself, the players and the club.

“But I will keep fighting until I’m told otherwise.

“There’s no hiding away from it. It was an unacceptable performance and an unacceptable result.

“We have to get players that want to fight and try to get us out of this situation.

“Ultimately, the blame will fall on me no matter what, and deservedly so at times.

“I’ll just keep fighting and working as hard as I possibly can.”

#2010. MN: Furious Amorim gave long speech to Milan squad after Ferencvaros loss – the details

Ruben Amorim held a discussion with the team after the full-time whistle in the defeat to Ferencvaros, a report has claimed.

Milan lost 2-0 to the Hungarian side at San Siro last night, further complicating their Europa League campaign. The current table reads just three points earned in four games, which has seen the Rossoneri drop out of the top 24 spots.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

More worrying than the result was the team’s performance. The first-half showing was slow and laboured, but even when the big names came on in the second half, the team never gave the impression of being able to mount a comeback.

The sloppy goals conceded are a clear reflection of everything that went wrong, with individual errors and an attitude that’s hard to explain, especially after the resounding win against Inter in the derby just a few days ago.

According to MilanNews, Amorim gave a long speech to the team in the dressing room after the match. There was a face-to-face discussion about this disappointing defeat and how it came about, including the wrong approach and numerous shortcomings in the overall management of the match.

It came after Amorim had given his thoughts on the game to Sky, speaking about a lack of desire and concentration, and about how he could not defend a performance like that despite normally going to bat for his players. A response is needed in Genoa on Sunday, or it could be a bitter break.

In the changing room he held everyone – including himself – accountable. The Portuguese also touched on some points that have been reiterated cyclically by various coaches since the post-Scudetto season.

Among these is the fact that Milan carry greater responsibilities than other clubs and that wearing the Rossoneri shirt is not a prize, but rather a new step in everyone’s career. The reference to how Strahinja Pavlovic trains was emblematic in identifying the Serbian as the standard to follow.

Obviously, Gerry Cardinale also wasn’t happy with the defeat against Ferencvaros, which comes after the derby victory and four days of work that made it even more emotionally impactful. The Milan owner is expected to return to Italy for Genoa-Milan on Sunday, and intends to further investigate the team’s ups and downs.

#2009. Falkirk sweat over ‘big player’ after injury mars Hearts rout

John McGlynn is hoping Brad Spencer is not facing a spell on the sidelines after the influential Falkirk captain was forced off with a knee injury in Sunday’s stunning 5-2 win at Hearts.

The rampant Bairns soared to third in the William Hill Premiership as they made it five top-flight victories on the spin for the first time since 1995.

But it may have come at a cost with Spencer having to go off in the 57th minute while his side led 5-1.

“Brad’s a big player to us,” said manager McGlynn, initially unsure of the extent of the injury. “We didn’t start the season particularly well and one of the reasons would be that Brad was suspended for the first two games of the season.

“He’s such an influence on us. And although we weren’t doing great in the second half (at Tynecastle), we certainly deteriorated once Brad went off.

“He’s such a calming influence and he made us tick. Once we got the couple of goals up, he managed to get on the ball, he was breaking the lines, he just looked like a class player.”

Asked whether Falkirk could maintain their stunning run of form, McGlynn said: “We’re delighted but we’re not going to get carried away, we’re 13 games in.

“There are other teams that have had good starts and are now maybe a little bit lower on the league table than where they were early on in the season.

“Apart from Hearts, virtually every other game we’ve played has been on a knife edge. Every game we’ve played in, you could win it, you could lose it, it could be a draw, and the league is very much like that.

“We’re delighted that we’re we’re getting that little edge that’s going in our favour, but I watch a lot of football, I understand what’s happening, and we’ve just got to try and keep getting the wee breaks.”

#2008. Little Common hold heads high despite defeat to Roffey

Having suffered a heavy 8-0 defeat against the same opposition on the opening weekend of the season, Common showed just how far they have progressed with a resolute display that kept them firmly in contention throughout.

The visitors enjoyed the lion’s share of possession during the opening period, but Common remained organised and difficult to break down, restricting Roffey's opportunities despite their territorial advantage. However, Common's resistance was finally broken on the stroke of half-time when a neat passing move from the visitors allowed Roffey to take a slender advantage into the interval.

The second half followed a similar pattern, with Roffey enjoying plenty of possession but finding clear-cut chances difficult to come by against a hardworking Common side.

Cruttwell was again called into action, producing an excellent save low to his left to prevent the visitors from doubling their advantage.

Despite spending long periods without the ball, Common continued to battle for every challenge and remained within touching distance of an equaliser as the contest entered its closing stages.

The home side's best opportunity arrived late on when Sam Ellis rose to meet a delivery into the area, but his header flashed across the face of goal and away to safety. It proved to be Common's final opportunity as Roffey held on to secure all three points.

Boss Russ Eldridge said: “I thought the lads put in a really disciplined and hard-working performance against a very good Roffey side. They are up near the top of the table for a reason and we knew we would have to work extremely hard without the ball.

“When you consider we lost 8-0 to them on the opening day of the season, I think today's performance shows how far we have come. We were organised, difficult to break down and, despite them having plenty of possession, I didn't feel they created too many clear-cut opportunities.

“It was disappointing to concede right on half-time because we had worked so hard to keep them out. We stayed in the game throughout the second half and always felt we might nick something.

“The effort and commitment from the players couldn't be questioned. We now need to build on these performances and start turning them into points. If we continue showing that level of determination and togetherness, I'm confident results will come.”

"To win back the momentum, the first win isn't about going out and playing the opponent out of the park. You have to earn and work for it and I think it was exactly the right way with this hard-fought and well-deserved win to win the momentum back.

"Especially heading into the international break, it was very important."

Match-winner Okafor scored just 97 seconds after entering the fray. It was the fastest Premier League goal scored by a substitute this term.

On the impact of Okafor, who had been struggling with an abductor issue in recent weeks, Farke said: "Credit to our medical department and also to Noah, he has worked in a very, very disciplined fashion, 24 hours a day more or less to be available.

"With a few concerns of the medical department, they said (on Friday): 'Boss, Listen, if you want to use him, you have to make sure that you stay unbelievably disciplined and you can't bring him on longer than 15 or 20 minutes.'

On Gabriel Gudmundsson, who came off with a hamstring injury at the break, Farke added: "I hope that it's not too bad and hope to have him back on the other side of the international break."

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Arfield has been without a club since departing Livingston in May after taking on the role of caretaker player-manager for the final three matches of the 2025-26 season.

The move to Bayview represents a first full-time step into management for the former Canada international, who also had two spells with Falkirk as well as stints with Huddersfield Town, Burnley, Charlotte FC and Bolton Wanderers.

“I am absolutely delighted to be the new manager of East Fife and I cannot wait to get started,” Arfield, who has signed a contract until May 2029, told the club website.

“I feel I am ready to go into coaching after learning a lot from excellent managers during my playing career, and I am grateful to East Fife for believing in me and for giving me this opportunity.

“My aim is now to create opportunities for others and to build a team which will excite East Fife supporters and attract the attention of the local community. It is a highly respected club which has great potential, and it is a privilege to be given the chance to lead it forward.”

Liam Anderson, chairman of East Fife, added: “We are delighted to have agreed a deal with Scott to become our new player-manager.

“This an innovative appointment and gives a clear indication of our ambitions going forward. I am sure that the arrival of Scott will be welcomed by our fans who are keen to see an exciting brand of football at Bayview.”

Arfield, who played for Rangers in the Europa League final four years ago, will take charge of the Fifers for the first time when Peterhead visit Bayview on Saturday. He also hopes to resume playing this month once he regains match fitness.

An East Fife statement added: "The board of directors is grateful to the interim management team of Jim Moffat, Pat Slattery and Brian Easton, who have guided the squad through the recent period of vacancy. Jim will continue as goalkeeping coach, Pat will assist with coaching while injury prevents him from playing, and Brian returns to on-field duties."

Ferencvaros head coach Balazs Borbely has admitted that he was prepared for everything AC Milan threw at his side.

Milan went into the game hoping for a victory after losing two of their first three in the Europa League, and what followed was their worst performance under Ruben Amorim. Lenny Joseph’s second-half brace was enough for Ferencvaros to emerge with three points that their performance merited.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It was a rotated Rossoneri side again, as has been the trend in Europe, but even when Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira, Mario Gila and Luka Modric came on in the second half there was never the feeling that a comeback was happening.

Amorim made his thoughts clear after the game, while Balazs Borbely attended a press conference after what was a very memorable night for his side. They moved onto 12 points from 12 to begin their European campaign, and his words were relayed by MilanNews.

The fans chanted your name here at San Siro…

“I never thought things would turn out this way and that I would experience all this. Despite this, I want to send a message to our fans: they have been fantastic and we thank you so much for your support.

“I think all of Europe has heard about us, not just at home and in Hungary, so they can be proud too. Regarding your first question, I don’t even want to make too many comparisons between the two teams, about why we outclassed Milan.

“We had our game plan. We prepared for every single eventuality. We knew that Amorim often changes formations and that in the last five or six games they have played with both three and four-man defences.

“We were ready to react to both systems, to press in one way or another, to close down spaces and defend. We planned transitions for every eventuality, so I think the team came here prepared, motivated and with a healthy level of confidence, and this will show on the pitch.”

“We can be proud of both the result and the performance. I think it’s difficult to distinguish which was the best thing: both the result and the performance were excellent, so I couldn’t say, or at least I can’t decide, what we should be more proud of.

“At half-time, it was difficult to say anything because we were playing almost perfectly; you could say we put in an almost flawless performance for almost the entire half, not just in the first half.

“I just told the boys to keep playing the same way, there were only minor adjustments to be made, and I reiterated to them to keep working the same way. I knew, somehow I felt, that we would win.”

This match will be talked about even in 40-50 years…

“We probably still can’t fully grasp what happened. Maybe as time goes by, soon, when I think back on this match, the whole evening, the atmosphere, and our performance, I’ll feel incredibly emotional, but right now I’m still trying to fully experience this moment.”

You seemed more athletically ready than Milan…

“I joined the team around the beginning of July. I had an idea in mind, a vision of what my team should be like, and we’ve been working, and we continue to work constantly, since the summer, to ensure we can deliver a similar level of performance to today.

“Of course, there are less stellar days, and we always have mistakes that need to be corrected, that we need to fix, but we’re constantly working, training the players, and getting to know each other: the staff, the new arrivals, and the team.

“We always try to analyse day by day, identify mistakes, find what’s not working well, fix it, and move forward. And to improve every single day by at least 1%.”

“I haven’t looked back at my comments yet to understand exactly what happened and why he got the red card, but I feel sorry for Yusuf, because he’s a good guy and I’m sure he didn’t want to weaken his team.

“He was probably unlucky with his elbow, hitting his opponent in the face, which is why he was sent off. Mistakes are part of the game, they happen. Our reaction was perfect, in my opinion. Everyone knew there were 15 minutes left, that we had to defend, sacrifice ourselves, and fight for each other.

“I think the last fifteen to twenty minutes, including injury time, played out exactly as they should. I think that even in those fifteen minutes, we managed to create two important chances with Zachariassen and Marquinhos.

“So, starting with a solid and big defence, we managed to pose a threat towards the opponent’s goal even when we were ten men short, and, if I remember correctly, we conceded very few opportunities to our opponents.”

#2004. Little Common hold heads high despite defeat to Roffey

Having suffered a heavy 8-0 defeat against the same opposition on the opening weekend of the season, Common showed just how far they have progressed with a resolute display that kept them firmly in contention throughout.

The visitors enjoyed the lion’s share of possession during the opening period, but Common remained organised and difficult to break down, restricting Roffey's opportunities despite their territorial advantage. When the visitors did find a way through, goalkeeper Matt Cruttwell was in fine form, producing two smart saves to keep the scores level.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

However, Common's resistance was finally broken on the stroke of half-time when a neat passing move from the visitors allowed Roffey to take a slender advantage into the interval.

The second half followed a similar pattern, with Roffey enjoying plenty of possession but finding clear-cut chances difficult to come by against a hardworking Common side.

Cruttwell was again called into action, producing an excellent save low to his left to prevent the visitors from doubling their advantage.

Despite spending long periods without the ball, Common continued to battle for every challenge and remained within touching distance of an equaliser as the contest entered its closing stages.

The home side's best opportunity arrived late on when Sam Ellis rose to meet a delivery into the area, but his header flashed across the face of goal and away to safety. It proved to be Common's final opportunity as Roffey held on to secure all three points.

Boss Russ Eldridge said: “I thought the lads put in a really disciplined and hard-working performance against a very good Roffey side. They are up near the top of the table for a reason and we knew we would have to work extremely hard without the ball.

“When you consider we lost 8-0 to them on the opening day of the season, I think today's performance shows how far we have come. We were organised, difficult to break down and, despite them having plenty of possession, I didn't feel they created too many clear-cut opportunities.

“It was disappointing to concede right on half-time because we had worked so hard to keep them out. We stayed in the game throughout the second half and always felt we might nick something.

“The effort and commitment from the players couldn't be questioned. We now need to build on these performances and start turning them into points. If we continue showing that level of determination and togetherness, I'm confident results will come.”

#2003. Barnsley FC and Daniel Stendel welcomed fun back like an old friend in FA Cup win v Aldershot Town - analysis

As Daniel Stendel sat down to dissect Barnsley’s 7-2 FA Cup win over Aldershot Town, he offered a wry smile.

He had been asked about the two goals his side leaked late in a game that had already been taken well beyond the opposition.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It was a question he will have known was coming, and a question most managers would have enjoyed answering to demonstrate their forensic and demanding nature. The word ‘standards’ would have most likely been used.

Stendel, however, had no interest in poking holes in a mostly scintillating performance. And who could blame him?

Barnsley’s campaign has been largely devoid of fun and rife with simmering discontent. With Bonfire Night celebrations spilling over into the weekend, Stendel clearly felt the Reds needed to simply enjoy the sparks.

“We keep the positive things,” said Stendel. “It's normal that I think about the two goals, but I think we analysed a lot in the last couple of weeks about some situations, some games, and why we didn't win the game in the end.

“I think today is time to say ‘good result, we're in the hat for the next draw’.”

Barnsley flew out of the traps at a dizzying pace and the brakes were simply never applied. By half-time, Cameron McGeehan and Vimal Yoganathan braces and a Reyes Cleary effort had Aldershot dead and buried.

McGeehan completed his hat-trick after the break and Rylan Brownlie got in the act, with the latter rounding off the afternoon after Aldershot had twice hit back via Annisuis Lewis.

“It was good to see that we used the spaces that we get, and a goal after a set-piece.

“I think three goals after crosses was good, especially that. It's one thing that we try to change and what we train in training, why we said we have to cross more balls in the box. And yeah, it was good today.”

Toxicity has enveloped Oakwell in recent months and while it has not been Stendel’s doing, it is clear he is relishing the trickling return of some positivity.

His side’s hard-fought draw with Oxford United a week prior evoked nostalgia, memories of a first spell in which supporter connection was strong.

They did not require the same spirit against the Shots but bluntly, it was just nice to see some goalscoring fun. It is a pleasure with which the Oakwell faithful have not been well-acquainted of late.

“We needed this game,” said Stendel. “It's a good opportunity for everybody to prove what we want to do next week and to get some confidence in defence and offence for winning duels, try to do things, cross the ball early, and in the box you can score goals.

“We have tough weekends in the past, and I think it was good for everybody, for the mindset, for the training time next week, for the game, especially before the weekend game.”

Barnsley will host Oldham Athletic in the Jersey Mike’s Trophy on Wednesday (November 11) but it is clear Stendel’s primary focus is on the Brick Community Stadium. That is where Wigan Athletic will entertain the Reds in a battle of two of League One’s bottom four sides on Saturday (November 14).

A battling league draw followed by a thorough dismantling of an inferior FA Cup opponent represents a start - but it would take a league win for the phrase ‘turning point’ to be uttered with any conviction. At present, it can only be whispered.

“I think we play sometimes really well, but we get no points for that,” said Stendel. “You have to score, you have to defend.

“I think it's important that everybody looks for situations that you can score, not only our strikers.

“I think this is important, especially for the next weeks when we have some games against teams around our situation in the table, but also we talk a lot about our defence behaviour, we have to improve that, and I think it was a good step in the right direction today.”

#2002. Hearts unbeaten home record obliterated as swashbuckling Falkirk earn 31-year first

Rampant Falkirk obliterated Hearts’ 18-month unbeaten home record in the Scottish Premiership with a stunning 5-2 win at Tynecastle as they leapfrogged the Jambos into third place.

Wouter Vrancken’s beleaguered side, missing 11 players through injury amid a gruelling fixture list, were in disarray as the swashbuckling Bairns romped into a five-goal lead early in the second half through Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Hearts hit back through substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Claudio Braga penalty, but Falkirk were well worthy of making it five top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1995.

It was a first league defeat at Tynecastle for Hearts since April 2025. To exacerbate their grim predicament, the Jambos, who have won just two of their last 11 matches, lost yet another senior player as Malachi Fagan-Walcott limped off in the second half.

There were two changes to the Hearts side that started Thursday’s Conference League defeat to Thun as Stephen Kingsley and Guendouz were replaced by Yan Dhanda and Landry Kabore.

Falkirk boss John McGlynn, named manager of the month for October, made one enforced change from the side that defeated Celtic last Sunday as Jack McMillan took over from injured right-back Ryan Strain.

The Bairns seized the lead in the fourth minute. After Murrell’s close-range effort from Scott Tanser’s cross was brilliantly saved by Beau Reus, Barbrook reacted quickest to drill home a low, angled finish from eight yards out.

Hearts threatened an equaliser in the 10th minute, but Kabore’s effort on the turn from the edge of the six-yard box was superbly blocked by Scott Bain.

Falkirk doubled their lead in the 17th minute after the hosts were caught wide open on the counter-attack. Dhanda’s shot from distance was charged down, allowing the Bairns to break swiftly, with Brad Spencer weighting his pass perfectly for Eames, who fired past the exposed Reus.

Braga thought he had pulled one back for Hearts in the 20th minute, but it was ruled out for handball.

Falkirk took full advantage of this reprieve by adding a third in the 33rd minute as Murrell peeled off Fagan-Walcott at the back post to nod home Deniss Melniks’ cross from the right.

The visitors struck again in first-half stoppage-time as Henderson curled high past Reus after Tanser’s corner broke to him just inside the box.

As jeers rained down from an irate home support, Vrancken replaced midfielders Laurent Mendy and Dhanda with Guendouz and Matthew Gillies for the start of the second half.

But within two minutes of the restart Falkirk notched again as Murrell fired home after being set up by Ethan Ross.

Hearts got off the mark when Guendouz drilled in his first goal for the club from just inside the box in the 50th minute.

Braga then tucked away a penalty in the 74th minute after Guendouz was tripped by Lewis Neilson, but it was not enough to prevent a third straight defeat for the Jambos.

#2000. Jordan Thewlis dares to dream after Guiseley striker is the FA Cup hero against Sutton United

Thewlis' Guiseley had been the better side against a Sutton United team two divisions higher in the pyramid, but had yet to make it count.

When Zac Kennard-Kettle blew his whistle as Jack Tinker tumbled in the penalty area in the 86th minute, the home supporters in a 1,556 crowd roared their excitement. But it soon turned to disappointment when the referee signalled the foul came just outside the 18-yard box.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The free-kick was worked to Thewlis – like Tinker, a substitute – and ballooned into the night sky.

"I think VAR would have given a penalty,” smiled Thewlis. "We probably got... not robbed a little bit, but it was touch and go, wasn't it? You think everything's going against you.

"I think we got booked quite quickly where they might have not. I think the league team does get favoured slightly on occasions."

Thewlis had been denied his moment before. He equalised for Conference North Boston United in a 2019 round two replay against Rochdale, only to miss a huge day out.

"They were in League One," he recalls. "We drew away and then we played them on a Monday at home and lost to a late penalty, 2-1. The draw had been made so we knew we were going, it was Newcastle away.

"That was a bit of a killer, the closest I've come to a third round."

Because four minutes into a minimum of five added to a game already running 21 late because of a medical emergency, Thewlis picked the ball up on the left and bundled his way so close to goal that once the whistle went again, there was no doubt.

"Fair play to the ref for giving the pen because it would have been an easy one to wave away," said Thewlis of Jake Taylor's challenge.

"It was a bit like when we were schoolboys," said the 34-year-old’s manager, PE teacher Ian Richards. "He's won it, he takes it. Cam Wilson's our penalty-taker but Jordan's good from the penalty spot. I was very calm because it was him.

"He's played League Two, National League, National League North. He's made a career on scoring and coming inside like that, weaving through to get a shot off or a penalty."

According to Thewlis: "I just tried to keep my head as clear as possible. The free-kick a few minutes before that, I've sent nine miles in the air. (I was thinking) just don't do that.

"I was confident I'd score. I was confident he'd go the wrong way."

Northern Premier League Premier Division Guiesley’s 1-0 win over fifth-tier Sutton was fully deserved.

"Chances created, shots on target, we were the better team, possession probably evenish, although they might have edged it,” said Thewlis.

Sutton began stronger but their only shot on target was Omar Mussa’s from about 30 yards in the 92nd minute. It was right at Jack Hall.

As the Lions got on top, Elliot Owen missed a good header from a corner and left-back Ollie Brown put an excellent chance laid on by Jack Emmett beyond the far post.

“Usually if you don't take them you can get punished," reflected Thewlis. "But the chances kept coming."

And Richards made good use of a 36-minute half-time.

"I said don't let this affect you," he recalled. "You've got the momentum, try and get that momentum again.

"I talked about how the No 9 (Temi Babalola) would come on to be a bit more direct, which he did. And we picked up where we left off.

"Even though they moved the ball quicker, we looked more threatening. There were a couple of last-ditch tackles by them in the area and a lot of opportunities to score."

The game restarted as more of an arm wrestle. Usually, the last 20 minutes between full-time and part-timers favour the pros. Not here.

"If you get dominated from minute one to 70, 80, you're tired, but we weren't ," argued Thewlis, a property renovator by day.

"We pride ourselves on how hard we work the players in terms of pre-season and we make the training more about quality and high intensity than quantity," said Richards. "And we utilise the squad. I felt a bit of that, a bit of home advantage and a bit of adrenaline got us through."

"There's not many in our league that could put nine on the bench, never mind the quality that we've got," said Thewlis proudly.

Winger Amir Berchil grew in influence as legs tied and in Harrison Hopper had a midfielder to pick him out. He did well to go past Besart Topallaj in the 80th minute, but when the ball came to Kallan Murphy, he slipped. Sent clear in the first added minute, Berchil shot at Brits.

But Thewlis was not going to be denied again.

"I'd rather a winnable one – another National League team," was his answer to the obligatory question of who he would like in Monday's draw. "And at home, it gives us a chance, doesn't it? You start looking at the third round now.

"I'd rather get to that third round. I've never got to the third round."

Neither have Guiseley, beaten twice in the second.

Guiseley: Hall; Odunston, Owen, Mbeka, Brown (Thewlis 78); Hopper, Staniland; Wilson (White 78), Emmett (Tinker 57), Berchil (Iggulden 90+6); Murphy.

Unused substitutes: Roxburgh, Lund, Longbottom, Wadsworth, Sinfield.

Sutton United: Brits; Urpens (Nightingale HT), Kirk, Topalloj, Brookes; Osadebe (Mussa 78), Taylor; Folarin, Knight (Babalola 65), Francis (Ogbonna 65); Carter.

Unused substitutes: Bell, Haigh, Moore-Taylor, Njoku, Amartey.

​Day-night game: The time of year and 36-minute half-time break for a medical incident turned the match into a cricket-style day-nighter with the two halves played in contrasting conditions. But whatever light you looked at it, in, Guiseley were the better team.

Star performers: Ollie Brown missed a golden chance, but was otherwise excellent at left-back and in midfield, Harrison Hopper's passing was tremendous, Amir Berchil's wing-play got better as the gam went on and Jordan Thewlis won it from the bench, but all 15 Guiseley players who took to the field were lions.

Draw: The second round draw is on Monday at 6.45pm on TNT Sports and You Tube.

Brabin praised Sutton, who came through the club’s youth system, saying: “Will has been doing great this season, and I am delighted for him.”

Looking back on the match, Brabin said: “It was a proper cup tie and we are delighted to come out winners.

“When you look back on the match, I think we were deserved winners.

“We have been doing well recently and today reinforced that with a good performance and a good result.”

After an uneventful opening two thirds of the match, it suddenly exploded into life when Calum Kavanagh put Oldham ahead in the 66th minute with his sixth goal of the season.

Wrexham loanee and former Oldham forward Davis Keillor-Dunn equalised 10 minutes later with his fifth of the campaign before Sutton had the final word.

It was not the start Dave Challinor dreamt of from his first match as Owls manager.

He said: “I am really frustrated and disappointed not to have won.

“The first half was like a testimonial in being so slow – not like I want a team of mine to be.

“The substitutions changed the dynamics of the game – it would have been better if we had started that way.

“There is plenty of work to do – change won’t happen overnight but hopefully you saw some structure.”

#1997. Euro round-up: Barcelona fightback sinks Atletico Madrid as Inter Milan march on

A double from Fermin Lopez saw Barcelona come from behind to defeat Atletico Madrid 2-1 and restore their three-point lead at the top of LaLiga.

Real Madrid had drawn level with their rivals by beating Valencia on Saturday and it appeared Atletico might be the ones heading into the international break on top after Giuliano Simeone gave them a deserved early lead.

But Lopez equalised just before half-time and scored what proved to be the winner in the 66th minute as Barca cleared a major hurdle.

In Serie A, Inter Milan brought Como crashing down to earth as first-half goals from Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram earned them a 2-0 home win.

Como continued their remarkable debut season in Europe on Wednesday by thrashing Lens 9-1, but Cesc Fabregas’ side turned in a lacklustre display at San Siro as their six-game winning run in all competitions was halted.

The victory means Inter are only one point behind leaders Lazio, who drew 1-1 away to Napoli.

Equalisers from Nick Woltemade and Gleison Bremer earned Juventus a 2-2 draw against Fiorentina.

#1996. This is an embarrassment – Wouter Vrancken rages after Hearts humiliation

Wouter Vrancken condemned a “ridiculous” first-half display from his sorry Hearts side as their 18-month unbeaten home record in the Scottish Premiership was ripped apart by ruthless Falkirk.

The beleaguered Jambos, who went into the game without 11 players through injury following a gruelling run of fixtures, endured a dismal afternoon as the Bairns raced into a 4-0 half-time lead on their way to a 5-2 victory at Tynecastle.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double had the visitors 5-0 up within 47 minutes before Hearts reduced the deficit through substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Claudio Braga penalty.

It was a first league defeat at Tynecastle since April 2025 for the Jambos, who have now won just two of their last 11 matches in all competitions.

“This is an embarrassment, the first half for sure,” said Vrancken. “Always doubting, always doing things half-half, in possession, out of possession, everything, and such easy goals again.

“When you give those easy goals, then you cannot win a game. It’s childish goals and cannot happen on this level. Those simple things, they are the basics actually in these situations.

“It’s crazy, crazy, and everybody – me, staff, players – have to take responsibility in those things. This is ridiculous.”

To exacerbate their grim predicament, the Jambos lost yet another senior player as defender Malachi Fagan-Walcott limped off in the second half.

“This also makes me a bit angry, because now we lose Mal again,” said Vrancken.

“Hopefully it’s not too bad, but still we had to replace him there, because he was one of the guys who were good in the game and in the last games actually he had a really consistent, good level.”

Hearts were leapfrogged into third place by Falkirk, who made it five top-flight wins in a row for the first time in 31 years.

“I’ve never been 5-0 up here before,” said Bairns manager John McGlynn. “First half we were outstanding. A great start to the game for us to get the goal so early.

“It was well documented about the Hearts injuries and, coming off the back of the game on Thursday night (in Thun), it was always going to be difficult for them.

“We had to smell blood and we had to go for it and that’s exactly what happened. The goals and our play were outstanding in the first half. We won every duel, we won everything all over the park.

“We got ourselves 4-0 up at half-time, which is dreamland. At 3pm, we never expected to be 4-0 up at half-time and certainly not 5-0 up a few minutes into the second half, which was another really good goal in transition.

“Hearts had a lot at the ball and dominated the second period, but we’re taking 5-2 every day of the week, make no mistake about it. It jumps us up into third place.

“Winning five on the trot has not been done since 1995, Jim Jefferies’ team, so I’m delighted for everyone at the football club that we’ve managed to equal that record.”

#1995. Bexhill are too strong for Billingshurst

It felt like a long time since the Pirates had travelled to Billingshurst in early August for the first game of the season, and a tough challenge on their sun-baked, dustbowl of a pitch, which saw Bexhill come away 2-1 winners. This was a chance to chalk up the first double of the campaign.

Prior to kick off, the Polegrove rang out to the haunting strains of The Last Post as two minutes’ silence for Remembrance weekend was impeccably observed.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Bexhill certainly started with clear intent and on five minutes Luke Donaldson met a ball in at the near post from Ash Latuske and just failed to meet the target. Minutes later Latuske himself had a shot well saved by Trigwell in the Billingshurst goal.

Quarter of an hour in and Jack Shonk burst through on the run but clipped his shot wide. It felt like Bexhill needed to capitalise on the pressure they were creating and convert one of their chances and on 25 minutes the opening goal came.

Billingshurst were all at sea from a corner and it was Callum Brand on the spot to knock the chance into the net. Five minutes later Bexhill created a great chance to double the lead when Latuske swept down the flank and set up Connor Robertson who fired over.

But if Bexhill thought the game was in the bag they had another think coming as the closing phase of the first half proved to be the best part of the game for Billingshurst. Suddenly it was the home side on the back foot and with serious work to do at the back.

No game passes these days for the Pirates without Dale Penn being called upon to put his body on the line and on 37 minutes he threw himself across the six-yard box to clear a shot away at the death that looked for all the world like it was heading into the net.

It was a wake-up call for Bexhill as they went into the break and goal to the good. Attacking the favoured Brockley Road end in the second half they set about the task of putting the game to bed. But, again, they would have to be patient.

There was no shortage of creativity for the Pirates. And no shortage of chances.

On 55 minutes Trigwell pulled off the save of the day – tipping a Latuske volley on to the bar. Bexhill kept coming but were frustrated by some decent defending and it would be fair to say it was all Pirates in the second half.

On 85 minutes Theo Coombs, who had dropped deeper into midfield when Kyle Holden went off with a knock, got forward and drove a decent effort wide. A couple of minutes later Coombs got on the end of a great ball from Jack Mison and at last notched the second goal Bexhill had been chasing.

On the brink of full-time Charlie Scarles slapped the icing on the cake, breaking clear through the defensive line and tucking his chance calmly past the keeper.

A 3-0 scoreline was probably fair and gets Bexhill’s push to be contenders in the league’s chasing pack back on track.

On Saturday they are at home again in the league, with a 3pm kick off against Seaford Town.

Matteo Moretto has confirmed that Markus Krösche will look to try and bring Timmo Hardung with him to AC Milan.

In the past few days, there have been reports from a number of sources claiming that Gerry Cardinale is finally going to get the man that he has wanted for a few months. Krösche – who left Eintracht Frankfurt last month – has an agreement in place to come in and lead the management.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The issue of the compensation to be paid to Eintracht seems to have been resolved, so now the main question concerns whether someone will come in to help him as a sporting director, another position vacant in the current set-up.

In a video on their YouTube channel, Fabrizio Romano and Matteo Moretto gave some updates on the plans for Milan moving forward, including the restructuring of the management. MilanNews relayed the words of the latter.

“The Krosche deal has been a rollercoaster ride. AC Milan had practically already finalised the deal before the summer window. It was also a question of timing and also of finances, as Eintracht Frankfurt were asking for much higher compensation than what Milan has paid so far, or will soon pay,” he said.

“Anyway, here we go: Marcus Krösche will be ​​Milan’s new Head of Football. Milan will pay compensation of between €3-4m. Official confirmation, as far as I know, will arrive in early January. However, it’s clear that Krosche will already begin working behind the scenes for AC Milan in the coming months, and then he will officially be the new Rossoneri director from January.

“Krösche fits into an organisational and sporting structure that Cardinale had already thought of once he had restructured Milan from scratch. There are other figures within the Milan structure, such as Bobby Gardiner, Almstadt, who from what I understand will remain, but it is clear that Krosche’s figure will be predominant and on a sporting level he will be the one with the most power.

“From what I understand, Krösche continues to push to try to bring in a sporting director who can add to the organisational chart and the name that continues to buzz in Krösche’s head is certainly that of his right-hand man Timmo Hardung, who is the current sporting director of Eintracht. However, it is still to be seen whether Timo Hardung will remain at Eintracht 100%.

“It is true that Eintracht are trying to give him as much power as possible, but I do not rule out Hardung’s exit starting from January or February. Milan remain on the lookout, other German clubs such as Nürnberg, Hannover or Hamburg are also interested in Hardung. Milan wants try inserting another figure, maybe a little further forward.”
